UNIT.subject: Core Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Formation of quadratic expressions
• Quadratic identities derived from the concept of area: (a + b)², (a − b)², a² − b²
• Factorisation of quadratic expressions
• Formation of quadratic equations from real-life situations
• Solving quadratic equations by factorisation
• Application of quadratic equations in real-life situations

UNIT.focus: This unit uses a Kenyan farm-plot situation to show learners that quadratic expressions arise naturally from area. Learners move from area models to identities, factorisation and solving equations, then apply these to real contexts. Each lesson follows Predict, Observe, Explain, DQB and Model Building, so learners revise one cumulative model of quadratic relationships.
UNIT.phenomenon: A farmer in Kericho has exactly 40 m of fencing wire for a rectangular vegetable plot (sukuma wiki and spinach) beside her house. When her children try different widths, they notice that a plot 8 m wide and a plot 12 m wide both enclose exactly 96 m². A plot 10 m wide gives a larger area of 100 m², and any width above 20 m is impossible. Learners ask: with the same fence, why do two different shapes give the same area, why is there a maximum, and how can we find the widths for a target area without trial and error? Learners observe the pattern with string loops, grid paper and tile models and find that it is described by an expression with a squared term, a quadratic.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A path of uniform width around a rectangular maize shamba in Nakuru changes the total area in a way that is not simply proportional to the path width.
• A paving contractor in Kisumu notices that a square courtyard with a square cut out has area equal to a product of two sums, a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
• A mandazi vendor in Mombasa wants a rectangular tray whose length is 3 cm more than its width and whose area is 180 cm².
• A ball thrown by a school athlete at Kasarani passes the same height twice, once going up and once coming down.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use quadratic expressions and equations to find the dimensions of a plot when its fence length and area are both fixed, and why do two different plots sometimes have the same area?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS (not included in the supplied OCR text; verify wording against the KICD page):
1. How do we form quadratic expressions and equations?
2. Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Forming quadratic expressions. Learners predict how area changes with width for a 40 m fence, then use grid paper to build width × length expressions such as x(20 − x) and (x + 3)(x + 5). DQB: Why does the area follow a pattern with x²?
Lesson 2: Deriving identities from area. Learners use area tiles and cut-out squares to derive (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², and test them with plots of 10 m, 12 m and 8 m. Model v1: area models for expansions.
Lesson 3: Difference of two squares and applying identities. Learners cut a small square from a large square, rearrange the pieces to derive a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), and use it for quick mental calculations such as 52² − 48². Model revised with all three identities.
Lesson 4: Factorising x² + bx + c. Learners predict the dimensions of a rectangle from a given area expression, rebuild it with tiles, and factorise by finding two numbers with a given sum and product. Link back to the 8 m and 12 m plots.
Lesson 5: Factorising ax² + bx + c and special cases. Learners use the grouping method and the area-tile method to factorise expressions such as 2x² + 7x + 3, and check by expansion. DQB review: which methods work best, and when?
Lesson 6: Solving quadratic equations by factorisation. Learners use the zero-product idea to solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0 and explain why x = 8 and x = 12 both appear, resolving the central puzzle of the phenomenon. Model revised to include two solutions.
Lesson 7: Forming quadratic equations from real-life situations. Learners translate the mandazi tray, path-around-shamba and thrown-ball situations into equations and solve them, rejecting solutions that make no sense, such as negative lengths.
Lesson 8: Applying and synthesising. Learners use their full model to design a school-garden plot of a target area with a given fence length, justify their dimensions to the class, and explain the maximum area at 10 m. They finalise the DQB and the cumulative model.

LESSONS.title: Forming Quadratic Expressions from Areas: Mama Wanjiru's 40 m Fence
LESSONS.aresKeywords: quadratic expression, area model, width, length, expand, x² term, perimeter, fence, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: Learners meet the anchoring phenomenon of Mama Wanjiru's 40 m fence, predict how area changes with width, and learn to write a width × length area as an algebraic expression and expand it to reveal an x² term, recognising it as a quadratic expression.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to form quadratic expressions: (a) write the area of a rectangle as width × length using x for the width, (b) expand x(20 − x) = 20x − x² and (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15, and (c) recognise an expression whose highest power is 2 as a quadratic expression. This is part of Sub-strand 1.3 Quadratic Expressions and Equations (KICD Core Mathematics Grade 10, July 2025). Verify the exact KICD outcome wording against the KICD page.
slo.skills: Predicting from a pattern, modelling a plot with string loops and grid paper, building area tables, using variables to generalise (x and 20 − x), expanding brackets, and communicating reasoning in groups. NGSS-style practices embedded: asking questions, developing and using models, analysing and interpreting data, using mathematics to represent a phenomenon.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about why a fixed fence gives equal areas for different widths; willingness to test predictions and revise them; respect for each member's ideas in group work; responsibility in handling shared materials. Values and PCIs to be quoted verbatim from the KICD page, which has not been verified here.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? 2. Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? (KICD key inquiry questions; verify wording against the KICD page.) Lesson question: How does the area of Mama Wanjiru's plot change as the width changes, and why does an x² term appear?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launches the phenomenon. Mama Wanjiru in Kericho has exactly 40 m of wire for a rectangular sukuma wiki and spinach plot. Her children Chebet and Kiprop notice that widths of 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m², 10 m gives 100 m², and widths above 20 m are impossible. Learners build the expression x(20 − x), see the x² term appear, and open the DQB with the question 'Why does the area follow a pattern with x²?'. Later lessons will use the expressions formed here (the lesson map names the area models and the x² term). Nothing is solved here beyond seeing the pattern.
slo.safetyNotes: Cutting string and paper: use blunt-ended scissors and keep them on desks. Keep walkways clear while groups spread out grid paper. No outdoor work is needed. Make sure every learner can see and reach the materials and that seating allows all to participate.

LESSONS.overview: Teacher introduces Mama Wanjiru's problem: 40 m of wire for a rectangular plot beside her house in Kericho. Learners first predict, individually and then in pairs, how the area changes as the width changes (Predict). In groups they model the plot with 40 cm string loops (1 cm = 1 m) on 1 cm grid paper, record widths, lengths and areas in a table, and compare with the class table (Observe). They discover that 8 m and 12 m give the same 96 m² because they are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round, that 10 m gives the maximum 100 m², and that widths above 20 m are impossible. They then write the length as 20 − x, the area as x(20 − x), expand it to 20x − x², and use tiles to expand (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15, naming both as quadratic expressions (Explain). The class opens the DQB (DQB Creation) and sketches Model v0: a diagram with a fixed perimeter, width x, length 20 − x and the question marks about equal areas and the maximum (Model Building). Nothing in this lesson solves for x; solving is saved for later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners listen to the story: 'Mama Wanjiru in Kericho has exactly 40 m of wire to fence a rectangular plot for sukuma wiki and spinach beside her house.' Individually they write a prediction in their books: 'If she makes the plot 2 m wide, 10 m wide, then 20 m wide, what will happen to the area?' They sketch a rough graph or sentence for how area changes as width increases. In pairs they compare predictions and mark with a star the width they think gives the biggest area. Some will predict that wider always means bigger; some will predict a middle width is best.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw a rectangle on the board and say: 'Mama Wanjiru has exactly 40 m of wire. Where does the wire go?' (Take 2 answers; confirm the wire goes all the way round, so length + width = 20 m.) Say: 'Take two minutes of silent thinking. Write your own prediction before talking.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'If the plot is 2 m wide, how long is it?' Cold-call 3 learners for the length. Then ask: 'Which width do you think gives the biggest area? Write it down and give a reason.' Cold-call 4 pairs without telling them if they are right. Record all predictions in a column on the board headed 'Our predictions'. Say plainly: 'We will not decide who is right by opinion. We will test.' Do not reveal the area table yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with public prediction recording. Writing a prediction before seeing evidence commits learners to an idea, so that comparing it with the measured area table creates cognitive conflict and a need to explain. Recording all predictions on the board gives the class a shared reference to revisit in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners correctly state length = 20 − width, or at least that length and width add to 20 m (look at written predictions); (2) predictions include a reason, not just a number; (3) learners can say what changes and what stays fixed (perimeter fixed at 40 m). Note and tally learners who predict that the widest plot gives the largest area; plan to ask them about it in the Observe phase. Walk the room and tick a checklist during the pair talk.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners get a 40 cm string loop (1 cm stands for 1 m), 1 cm grid paper and a table: width x | length 20 − x | area. They shape the loop into rectangles on the grid paper with widths 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18 cm, read the length, count squares (or multiply) for the area and fill in the table. Each group is asked to try width 20 and widths above 20. They notice: 8 and 12 both give 96; 6 and 14 both give 84; 4 and 16 both give 64; 10 gives 100, the largest; at 20 the length is 0, so there is no plot; above 20 it cannot be made. They compare with their predictions. They are told that Chebet and Kiprop found the 8 m and 12 m equal areas on their own. A group shows that an 8 by 12 plot and a 12 by 8 plot are the same rectangle turned round.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out materials and say: 'One centimetre stands for one metre. Your loop is Mama Wanjiru's whole 40 m of wire. Every rectangle must use the whole loop.' Demonstrate one width (x = 2, length 18, area 36) and then let groups work. Circulate and ask: 'How did you get the length without measuring it?' and 'What do the width and length always add up to?' After 8 minutes ask groups to fill in a class table on the board, one row per group. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then ask: 'What do you notice about the area column?' Cold-call 4 learners for noticing statements. Ask: 'Chebet and Kiprop say 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m². Are those two different plots?' Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners, then state plainly: 'It is the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round, not two different shapes.' Ask: 'What happens at width 20, and what about 22?' Cold-call 3. Note that a 4 m by 24 m plot also has area 96 m² but needs 56 m of wire, so it does not fit this fence. Return to the predictions on the board and ask learners to mark which were supported.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern noticing (noticing and wondering). Learners generate their own data with a physical model, then look for patterns across rows (symmetry about 10, a maximum of 100, impossible widths). Producing the data themselves makes the later algebra a way of explaining something they have already seen, not an abstract rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners fill in length as 20 − width without re-measuring after 2 or 3 rows; (2) area values in tables match the anchor table (36, 64, 75, 84, 96, 100, 96, 84, 75, 64, 36); (3) learners describe the symmetry in their own words (pairs of widths adding to 20 share an area); (4) learners explain that width 20 gives no plot. Check group tables for errors and ask the group to recount squares, not just correct them yourself. Record which groups notice the maximum at 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners ask: 'Can we write a rule for any width, not just the ones we tried?' With teacher guidance they let width = x m, length = (20 − x) m, and area A = x(20 − x). They expand using the grid: x(20 − x) = 20x − x², seeing that one term has x squared, since x times x is a square of side x. They check it with x = 8: 20 × 8 − 64 = 96. They then use area tiles (an x² tile, x strips, unit squares) to model a different rectangle (x + 3) by (x + 5) and expand it: x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15. They learn that an expression whose highest power is 2 is a quadratic expression, and they classify examples: 20x − x², x² + 8x + 15, 3x + 7 (not quadratic), x² (quadratic), x³ + 2 (not quadratic).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our table only covers some widths. If Chebet says 9.5 m, how would we find the area quickly?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Write on the board: width = x, length = ?, area = ? and ask learners to complete it in pairs (1 minute). Cold-call 2 pairs for the length 20 − x and the area x(20 − x). Ask: 'Use what you did in Grade 9 to expand x(20 − x). Which term is new?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners; write 20x − x² and circle the x² term. Ask learners to test x = 8 and x = 12 in 20x − x² and say what they notice (both give 96). Next, draw a large rectangle with sides (x + 3) and (x + 5) divided into four parts and ask groups to label the area of each part (x², 5x, 3x, 15). Ask: 'What do we get when we add the parts that are alike?' Cold-call 3 for x² + 8x + 15. Introduce the term 'quadratic expression' and give the rule: the highest power of x is 2. Give 5 quick examples for thumbs up or down. Say plainly that we have only written the area as an expression; we have not yet solved for any width.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete-representational-abstract progression with an area model. The string loop and table (concrete) lead to the grid and tile diagrams (representational) and then to the algebraic expression (abstract). The same rectangle is shown in all three forms, so learners see that the x² term comes from the square-shaped region of the diagram and is not an arbitrary algebra rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners write length as 20 − x and area as x(20 − x) without help; (2) learners expand x(20 − x) to 20x − x² and not 20 − x² or 20x + x²; (3) learners label all four regions of the (x + 3)(x + 5) diagram correctly and combine 5x + 3x = 8x; (4) learners correctly sort quadratic from non-quadratic expressions (a thumbs up or down check on 5 examples, aim for at least 80% correct). Follow up privately with learners who give 20 − x² and ask them to re-draw the grid. Use a 2-question exit slip: expand x(12 − x) and (x + 2)(x + 4).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write questions that this lesson has raised on sticky notes or slips, one question per slip, and stick them on the class DQB under the heading: 'How can we find the plot dimensions when fence length and area are both fixed, and why do two different widths sometimes give the same area?' Possible learner questions: Why does the area go up and then come down? Why does 10 m give the biggest area? Why do 8 and 12 give the same area? Can we find the width for a given area without trial and error? Why does the x² appear? What if Mama Wanjiru had 60 m of wire? They sort questions into groups such as 'Why equal areas?', 'Why a maximum?', 'How to find widths for a target area?', and 'What is x²?'
framework.teacherMoves: Put up the DQB chart paper with the driving question in the centre. Say: 'Think about what you still wonder. Write one question per slip. You have 3 minutes.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before circulating. Give each learner at least one slip and cold-call 5 learners to read their question aloud before sticking it up. Ask: 'Which of these questions might we be able to answer with the x² idea?' and cold-call 2 learners. Help the class cluster the questions and label each cluster with a heading. Highlight the question the storyline gives for this lesson: 'Why does the area follow a pattern with x²?' If no learner has asked it, add it yourself and say 'I wondered this too.' Keep the DQB visible and say that later lessons will return to it. Do not answer questions now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering. Collecting learners' own questions gives them ownership of the unit, makes unresolved puzzles visible, and gives the class a way to track what has been explained later. Clustering shows learners how separate questions relate to the same underlying idea.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each learner contributes at least one question; (2) at least some questions refer to the phenomenon (equal areas, the maximum, the fixed fence) and not only to procedures; (3) learners can say which cluster their question belongs to and why. Note learners who write only 'how do I expand?' type questions and prompt them to link to the plot. Photograph or copy the DQB so the class can compare it with the final DQB.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners draw an initial class model, Model v0, in their books and on a large sheet: a rectangle labelled with width x and length 20 − x, the fixed 40 m perimeter, and the area expression x(20 − x) = 20x − x². Beside it they add a small table of widths and areas (2 to 18 m) and arrows marking what they know (equal areas at 8 and 12, the maximum at 10, no plot at 20) and question marks for what they cannot yet explain (why equal, why a maximum, how to find widths for a target area). In pairs they write a one-sentence 'What I know so far' and 'What I still need to find out'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must show what stays the same and what changes when the width changes.' Ask: 'What stays fixed? What changes?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Build Model v0 on the board using learner suggestions and make sure it has: the rectangle, x, 20 − x, the 40 m perimeter, the expression 20x − x², and the table. Ask learners to put question marks where the model cannot yet explain the observations. Cold-call 3 pairs for their 'still need to find out' sentence and link each to a DQB cluster. Close with: 'Today we wrote area as an expression with an x². Next time we will use area models to see why squares behave the way they do.' Collect the exit slip (expand x(12 − x) and (x + 2)(x + 4)) as learners leave. Keep Model v0 on the wall for revision in later lessons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building with explicit gaps. Learners draw and label a model that captures only what the evidence so far supports, and mark what it cannot explain. Showing gaps in the model gives purpose to later lessons and teaches learners that models are revised as evidence grows.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the model shows a rectangle with x and 20 − x labelled and the perimeter 40 m stated; (2) the area expression is written correctly as x(20 − x) = 20x − x²; (3) at least one question mark is placed where the model cannot yet explain a pattern (for example, the equal areas or the maximum); (4) exit slip: at least 80% of learners expand x(12 − x) = 12x − x² and (x + 2)(x + 4) = x² + 6x + 8 correctly. Use exit slip results to decide who needs extra practice with expanding before Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did learners fill in the length as 20 − x with understanding, or just copy the pattern? (2) Could learners say plainly that 8 m by 12 m and 12 m by 8 m are the same plot? Who still thinks they are different shapes? (3) Did anyone confuse x(20 − x) = 20x − x² with 20 − x²? What did the grid diagram do to help? (4) Which learners predicted that the widest plot has the largest area, and did the table change their minds? (5) Did the DQB contain questions that link to the phenomenon, or mostly procedure questions? (6) Did groups run short of grid paper, string, or time, and what will you change? (7) Which learners need extra support with expanding brackets before Lesson 2? Note two changes for next time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What we observed: With 40 m of wire, length + width = 20 m. Widths of 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m² (the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round), a width of 10 m gives the largest area of 100 m², and widths of 20 m or more do not give a plot.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What we learned: If the width is x m then the length is (20 − x) m and the area is x(20 − x) = 20x − x². Expanding (x + 3)(x + 5) gives x² + 8x + 15. An expression whose highest power is 2 is a quadratic expression.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: What we can explain so far: The x² term appears because multiplying a width x by a length that also contains x makes an x by x square region in the area model, so the area is a quadratic expression. We cannot yet explain why areas repeat in pairs, why the maximum is at 10 m, or how to find widths for a target area without trial and error; these questions go on the DQB.

LESSONS.title: Deriving the Squares Identities from Area: Why 12² = (10 + 2)² and 8² = (10 − 2)²
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; extend to a double period if learners cut and paste their own tile sets)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: identity, (a + b)², (a − b)², area model, cut-out square, expansion, perfect square, quadratic expression, Kericho plot, Model v1

slo.purpose: Learners use area tiles and cut-out squares to derive the identities (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², then test them on the squares 12² = (10 + 2)² = 144, 8² = (10 − 2)² = 64 and 10² = 100, which link to the plot widths in Mama Wanjiru's fencing problem.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to derive the quadratic identities (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² from the concept of area. An identity is true for all values of a and b. Learners also see how the identities fit the area models and expansions from Lesson 1.
slo.skills: Constructing and using area models (SEP: Developing and Using Models); making and testing a prediction with numbers (SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); communicating a general pattern in words and symbols (SEP: Constructing Explanations); cutting and measuring accurately.
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (learners explain why a middle term 2ab appears); Communication and Collaboration (learners justify their models to peers). Values: Integrity (record the cut and measured areas honestly, even when a check does not match at first); Responsibility (care for shared tiles, scissors and grid paper). PCI: Education for Sustainable Development, using scrap paper, old calendars and cardboard from the immediate environment for tiles.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? 2. Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? (KICD wording to be verified against the KICD page.) Lesson focus: How can area pictures help us write a squared bracket as a quadratic expression, and what do they tell us about Mama Wanjiru's plots?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 showed that the area of Mama Wanjiru's plot, x(20 − x) = 20x − x², is a quadratic expression, and that 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m². This lesson gives learners a tool for squared brackets, (a + b)² and (a − b)², that they will need to see why a square is the biggest possible plot. It starts Model v1, area models for expansions. Lesson 3 adds a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) and Lesson 4 runs expansion backwards to factorise. This lesson does not factorise and does not solve equations.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors and rulers: cut away from the body and carry them point-down. Use paper, card or old calendars only, with no blades or craft knives. Keep the floor clear of offcuts, and collect scraps in a bag for reuse or recycling. Learners with limited hand control may use pre-cut tiles or a partner to cut.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru in Kericho has 40 m of wire. Her children Chebet and Kiprop found that widths of 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m², while a 10 m by 10 m square gives 100 m². Learners already know the plot area x(20 − x) = 20x − x² is quadratic. In this lesson they ask: what happens when we square a bracket such as (10 + 2)² or (10 − 2)²? Learners first predict 12² and 8² from the square of 10. Then they build a 10 + 2 square from tiles (a 10 × 10 square, two 10 × 2 strips and a 2 × 2 square) and a 10 − 2 square by cutting away from a 10 × 10 square. They write the general identities, test them on 12², 8² and 10², and record the pictures as Model v1. 12 m and 8 m are the length and width of the same rectangle, the 8 m by 12 m plot turned round. The squares are used only as number tests of the identities. A key conclusion is that (a + b)² is not a² + b²: the middle strips 2ab are what the shortcut misses. Learners add questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and start Model v1.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Lesson 1: Mama Wanjiru's plot has area x(20 − x) = 20x − x², and widths of 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m². Each learner writes individually, on a sticky note or in their exercise book, a prediction for: (1) 12² if they only know 10² = 100; (2) 8² if they only know 10² = 100; (3) is (10 + 2)² equal to 10² + 2²? Yes or no, and why? They record a prediction and a reason in 'I think … because …' form. Then they pair-share and mark each prediction with a tick or a question mark.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board: 'Mama Wanjiru's plot can be 10 m wide, or 12 m, or 8 m. We know 10² = 100.' Say: "Without a calculator, write down what you think 12² is, and tell me why." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before any talking. Say: "Now turn to your partner and compare. Do not tell me who is right yet." Cold-call 3 pairs. Record every prediction, right or wrong, on the board without comment. Ask: "Who thinks (10 + 2)² = 10² + 2² = 104? Raise a hand. Who disagrees?" Count hands and write the numbers on the board. Say: "We will test this with real areas today." Do not give the answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): Writing a prediction first exposes the common misconception that (a + b)² = a² + b². Learners hold a clear claim to test, so the tile evidence in the Observe phase is a real test, not a lecture.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and note on a class tally: (1) how many learners predict 12² = 100 + 4 = 104 (the a² + b² misconception); (2) whether reasons mention area, squares or 'adding'; (3) learners who leave the reason blank or say 'just guessing'. Those who predict 104 are flagged for the middle strips. Indicator: at least 80% of learners write a prediction with some reason before the Observe phase begins.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners get a pack of paper tiles (cut from old calendars or exercise-book covers): one 10 cm by 10 cm square (a²), two 10 cm by 2 cm strips (ab), and one 2 cm by 2 cm square (b²). 1 cm stands for 1 m in the plot model. Part A, (a + b)²: Learners fit the four pieces together to make a bigger square of side 12 cm, then measure the side, record that 10 + 2 = 12, and count or calculate the total area as 100 + 20 + 20 + 4 = 144 cm². They compare with 12 × 12 = 144 and with their prediction. Part B, (a − b)²: Each group takes a fresh 10 cm by 10 cm square on grid paper and marks a border strip 2 cm wide along the top and along the right edge. They cut away the L-shaped border (two 10 × 2 strips overlapping at a 2 × 2 corner), leaving an 8 cm by 8 cm square. They count the area left: 64 cm². They compare with 100 − 20 − 20 + 4 = 64 (the corner 2 × 2 was removed twice, so it is added back once). They fill in a table: square, side, area from pieces, area from side × side. Also, they fill in a final line: side 10, area 100.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute tile packs and say: "Handle the scissors with care and cut away from your body." Model the first placement under the document camera or on the board: "Start with the big square, then add the two strips, then the little corner square. What shape do you get?" Circulate to every group within the first 5 minutes. Ask: "Where is the 2 × 2 piece in the picture? Why is it needed?" Then ask: "How many strips of 10 × 2 do you have? Why two and not one?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. For Part B, say: "When you cut away both strips, what did you take away twice?" Cold-call 2 groups to show the overlapping corner. Remind groups to record honestly: "If your measurement is 143 or 145, write what you measured and tell me why you think it is slightly off." Collect results from all groups onto a class table on the board. Link back: "12 m and 8 m are the length and width of the same plot turned round, and 10 m wide is the square."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Area Model Construction (physical modelling): Making a bigger square from four labelled pieces, then a smaller square by cutting from a larger one, lets learners see the middle terms 2ab as real strips. Learners build meaning from the geometry before the algebra is written.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group: (1) names each tile piece as a² (10 × 10), ab (10 × 2), ab (10 × 2) and b² (2 × 2); (2) arrives at 144 cm² from pieces and from 12 × 12; (3) arrives at 64 cm² for the 8 cm square after cutting; (4) points to the overlapped corner in Part B. Indicator: at least 3 of 4 learners per group can explain where the two ab strips are in the picture. Note groups that count 104 and stop; guide them with 'Did the strips fit?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners move from numbers to letters. In their groups they replace 10 with a and 2 with b, and write the area of the big square in two ways: as (a + b)² and as the sum of the pieces a² + ab + ab + b² = a² + 2ab + b². They write the same for the cut-out square: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². They then test the two identities on 12², 8² and 10²: (10 + 2)² = 100 + 40 + 4 = 144, (10 − 2)² = 100 − 40 + 4 = 64, and 10² = 100 (b = 0, the middle strips vanish). They write a short answer to: 'Why is (10 + 2)² not 10² + 2²?' Finally they connect to the phenomenon in a one-line statement: 'The 12 m width and 8 m width are the same plot turned round; their squares are tested here only as numbers.' They also try with x: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9, and compare it with Lesson 1's (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "If the big side is a and the small side is b, what are the areas of the four pieces?" Write answers as learners give them. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners for the four areas. Say: "An identity is true for ALL values of a and b, not only 10 and 2. How could we check that?" Invite 2 learners to try different numbers, such as a = 5 and b = 1: (5 + 1)² = 36 and 25 + 10 + 1 = 36. Ask: "In the 12 m case, where is the extra 40 in 144 = 100 + 40 + 4?" Expect: the two strips. Then say: "So who was right about 104?" Return to the Predict tallies and revisit them. For the minus identity ask: "Why does the b² come back with a plus sign?" Expect: the corner was cut away twice, so it is added back once. Briefly link: "In Lesson 1 we expanded (x + 3)(x + 5). Today's identity is the special case where both brackets are the same." Do NOT introduce a² − b² (Lesson 3) or factorisation (Lesson 4).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with generalisation: Learners state the general claim (the identity), give evidence (the tile counts and the tests with 144, 64 and 100) and give reasoning (the middle strips, the double-cut corner). Moving from a specific number to letters builds the abstraction step by step.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each group's identity statements and the answer to 'why not 10² + 2²?'. Look for: (1) both identities written correctly; (2) 2ab explained by the two strips; (3) + b² in the minus identity explained by the double-cut corner; (4) all three tests (144, 64, 100) calculated correctly. Indicator: at least 75% of learners write a correct explanation. Quick check on whiteboards: "Expand (x + 3)²." Expect x² + 6x + 9. Common error: x² + 9 or x² − 6x + 9. Reteach with a tile picture for these learners.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add sticky notes to the class DQB under the driving question about dimensions of the plot, fence length and area, and equal areas. They place new notes on: 'What we figured out today' (e.g. 'Squaring a bracket gives a middle term 2ab, not just a² + b².') and 'What we still wonder' (e.g. 'Can we cut a small square from a big square and rearrange it?', 'How do we go backwards, from x² + 8x + 15 to brackets?', 'Why is the biggest area exactly when the plot is a square?'). Each learner writes at least one question. Learners group related questions and mark the ones this lesson answered, such as 'Why do squares have a middle term?', with a tick.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take one sticky note. Write one thing we learned about squares and one question that is still open. You have 2 minutes." Circulate and read over shoulders. Cold-call 4 learners to read a note aloud and place it on the board. Ask: "Is this a question we can answer from area models, or do we need a new idea?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Point out good questions that link to the phenomenon: "Several of you asked why the square gives the biggest area. We will come back to that, and in Lesson 8 we will see why 100 m² is the maximum." Move answered questions to a 'Partly answered' column. Do not answer the future-lesson questions now; just say which lesson will take them up (difference of squares is next lesson; going backwards is Lesson 4).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (questioning and tracking): Writing, sorting and ticking questions shows learners their growing understanding and keeps the storyline coherent. The open questions point toward the next lesson's investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan the DQB notes: (1) at least 80% of learners add a note; (2) questions refer to the phenomenon, equal areas or the maximum, not only to procedures; (3) learners tick questions they can now answer. Indicator: at least 5 questions that relate to the next lessons (difference of squares, factorising, the 8 and 12 m solutions). If questions are only 'Is it on the exam?', prompt: "What would you like to know about Mama Wanjiru's plot?"

framework.learnerExperience: Learners start Model v1 on a large chart: area models for expansions. They draw (1) the Lesson 1 area rectangle for x(20 − x) = 20x − x² with a short label, (2) the (a + b) square split into a², ab, ab, b², with a = 10 and b = 2 and area 144, (3) the (a − b) square with the cut border, a = 10 and b = 2 and area 64, and (4) the square with side 10 and area 100. Under each picture they write the identity or expression. They add a line 'Plots 8 m and 12 m are the same rectangle turned round; 10 m by 10 m is the square' and a 'Not yet explained' box with two questions from the DQB. Each learner copies Model v1 into their own exercise book. Then each learner writes one sentence in a Model Prompt: 'Our model shows … It does not yet explain …'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Our model is a first draft. It will change in the next lessons. What must be on it so far?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to suggest one element each. Model the layout under the document camera: pictures at the top, identities in the middle, 'Not yet explained' at the bottom. Say: "Make sure each picture has its numbers labelled: 10, 2, 144, 64, 100." Circulate and check labels. Ask: "Where in your model can I see why 12² is bigger than 10²?" (The extra strips and corner are added.) "Where can I see why 8² is smaller?" (The border strips are removed, with the corner returned once.) Collect the 'does not yet explain' statements and read 2 aloud. Close with a preview: "Next lesson we cut a small square out of a large one and rearrange the pieces, and the 52² − 48² puzzle will follow." Do not write a² − b² on the model yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Model v1): Building the first version of a class model that is revised in later lessons shows learners how scientific and mathematical ideas grow. Naming what the model cannot yet explain keeps the driving question open and motivates the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: (1) the three area pictures drawn and labelled correctly; (2) both identities written correctly; (3) the statement that 8 m and 12 m are the same plot turned round; (4) at least one honest 'not yet explained' item. Indicator: at least 80% of learners can complete the model prompt sentence correctly. Exit ticket on one half-page: "Expand (x + 4)² using a tile picture or the identity." Expect x² + 8x + 16. Sort the tickets into correct, middle term missing and sign error, and plan a short reteach at the start of Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) How many learners moved from 'a² + b²' to the full a² + 2ab + b²? What in the tile evidence changed their minds? (2) Did groups correctly explain why b² is added back in (a − b)²? If not, would a coloured overlap help next time? (3) Did all learners link the identities back to Mama Wanjiru's plot and understand that 8 m and 12 m are the same rectangle turned round? Did anyone say they were 'different shapes'? (4) Did every learner get a turn to handle tiles, or did a few dominate? How will you re-balance roles in Lesson 3? (5) Which DQB questions need to be addressed in the next lesson, and which could confuse learners if not handled with care? Record 2 actions for Lesson 3.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built a 12 cm square from a 10 × 10 square, two 10 × 2 strips and a 2 × 2 square, and found its area is 144. We cut a 2 cm border from a 10 cm square and left an 8 cm square of area 64. The 10 cm square has area 100.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: An identity is true for all values. (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². The middle term 2ab comes from two strips, so (a + b)² is not a² + b². In (a − b)², the b² is added back because the corner was cut away twice.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The squares 12² = (10 + 2)² = 144, 8² = (10 − 2)² = 64 and 10² = 100 agree with the identities. The 8 m and 12 m widths are the same plot turned round. Model v1 shows area pictures for expansions, and it does not yet explain why 100 m² is the largest area or how to find both widths for a target area.

LESSONS.title: Cutting a Small Square from a Large Square: Difference of Two Squares
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; Predict 5, Observe 12, Explain 10, DQB 5, Model 8)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), identity, area model, mental calculation, 52² − 48², perimeter 40 m, Mama Wanjiru, Kericho plot, 100 − (x − 10)², cumulative model

slo.purpose: Learners derive the identity a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) by cutting a small square from a large square and rearranging the pieces into a rectangle. They then use it for quick mental calculation (52² − 48² = 4 × 100 = 400) and see how it links back to the Kericho plot, where the 40 m fence gives length 20 − x and area x(20 − x). The class cumulative model is revised so that it holds all three identities.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) derive a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) from an area model; (2) state, with the other two identities, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; (3) use a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) to calculate quickly, for example 52² − 48² = (52 − 48)(52 + 48) = 4 × 100 = 400; (4) see, as a preview only, that 100 − (x − 10)² = (10 − (x − 10))(10 + (x − 10)) = (20 − x)(x) = x(20 − x), the area of the Kericho plot.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): cutting and rearranging paper squares and drawing area diagrams. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): comparing the direct calculation 2704 − 2304 with the identity method. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): explaining why the L-shaped region becomes a rectangle with sides (a − b) and (a + b). Using mathematics (SEP 5): substituting numbers into an identity. KICD core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration; Creativity and imagination.
slo.attitudes: Learners show Responsibility by handling scissors carefully and keeping paper offcuts for the cumulative model. They show Integrity by cutting and measuring accurately. They show Respect by listening to each partner's explanation. PCI: Education for Sustainable Development, by reusing old exercise-book paper, and Life Skills, by making quick mental estimates in daily trade at a Kericho kiosk.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? (KICD key inquiry questions, to be verified against the KICD page.) Lesson question: How can cutting a small square out of a large square give us a shortcut for calculating, and how does it connect to the area of Mama Wanjiru's plot?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 taught how to write a width × length area as an algebraic expression and expand it to see an x² term. Lesson 2 derived (a + b)² and (a − b)² from area tiles and cut-out squares. Lesson 3 adds the third identity, a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), by cutting one square out of another. The class model of the plot is revised to include all three identities. The link 100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x) is only previewed here, since its full use in explaining the maximum of 100 m² comes in Lesson 8. Lesson 4 will run expansion backwards to factorise x² + bx + c.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors: cut away from the body, pass them handle first, and keep them on the desk when not in use. Cut only along ruled lines on paper. Paper offcuts should be collected in a tray so no one slips on them. Use no string loops this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Anchoring phenomenon: Mama Wanjiru in Kericho has exactly 40 m of fencing wire for a rectangular vegetable plot (sukuma wiki and spinach), so length + width = 20 m. Her children Chebet and Kiprop found that widths of 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m², that 10 m gives the largest area of 100 m², and that widths above 20 m are impossible. So far the class has written the area as x(20 − x) = 20x − x² (Lesson 1) and built (a + b)² and (a − b)² from area models of squares, testing 12² = 144, 8² = 64 and 10² = 100 (Lesson 2). In this lesson learners predict what remains when a small square is cut from a corner of a large square, then cut, rearrange and measure the pieces to discover that the L-shape becomes a rectangle with sides (a − b) and (a + b). They apply the result to 52² − 48² = 4 × 100 = 400 as a mental shortcut, and see a preview that 100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x): the plot area is a 10 m square with a small square taken away. The class revises its cumulative model so it holds all three identities.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the plot model from Lessons 1 and 2. Each learner silently writes a prediction in their exercise book: 'A square of side 10 cm has a square of side 4 cm cut from one corner. What is the area left? Can you think of a way to write it as one product of two lengths?' They calculate 100 − 16 = 84 cm² and sketch where they think the L-shape could be cut into a rectangle. Then, as a mental-maths challenge, they predict how long it would take to work out 52² − 48² without a calculator and give a guess of the answer. Many will square both numbers (2704 − 2304); this is recorded as their starting strategy.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the 10 cm square with a 4 cm corner removed on the board. Say: 'Remember Mama Wanjiru's plot in Kericho. In Lesson 2 we used squares of 12, 8 and 10 to test our tiles. Today we ask what happens when a small square is taken from a big one.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Write your prediction, then draw how you would cut this L-shape.' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after each question before anyone speaks. Cold-call 3 learners to share different cut ideas without judging them. Then write on the board: 52² − 48² = ? Ask: 'Without a calculator, how would you do it?' Cold-call 2 learners and record their methods. Say: 'Keep your predictions, we will test them with scissors.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Elicit Prior Ideas. Writing a prediction first commits learners to an idea that evidence can later confirm or change. Recording the 'square both numbers' strategy creates a need for a shortcut, so the identity is discovered as a solution to a real problem.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) does the learner calculate 100 − 16 = 84 correctly? (2) does the sketch show any attempt to rearrange the L-shape? (3) does the learner recall from L2 that squares can be modelled with areas? (4) how many learners use the 'square both numbers' method for 52² − 48²? Tally on the board. Learners who cannot find the L-shape area get a grid-paper square to count unit squares.

framework.learnerExperience: In pairs, learners use old exercise-book paper and rulers. Step 1: draw and cut out a large square of side a = 10 cm. Step 2: from one corner mark and cut out a small square of side b = 4 cm. Label the remaining L-shape with a² − b² and calculate its area, 100 − 16 = 84 cm². Step 3: cut the L-shape along a straight line (a dotted line is drawn from the inner corner to the outside edge) into two rectangles: one measuring 10 cm by 6 cm and one measuring 4 cm by 6 cm. Step 4: rotate the 4 cm by 6 cm rectangle and join it to the 10 cm by 6 cm rectangle so that the pieces form one long rectangle. Measure its sides: 6 cm (a − b) by 14 cm (a + b). Area = 6 × 14 = 84 cm², the same as the L-shape. Step 5: repeat with a second pair of squares of their own choosing (for example a = 9 and b = 5, giving 4 × 14 = 56 = 81 − 25) and record both in a table with columns a, b, a² − b², (a − b), (a + b), (a − b)(a + b). Finally learners write the general rule in symbols.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute scrap paper, rulers and scissors and review safety: 'Cut away from your body, pass scissors handle first.' Circulate and ask each pair: 'What is the area of the piece you cut away? What is left?' Prompt: 'Which sides of your new rectangle are made from a and b? How do you know?' Do not give the formula. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after each prompt. If a pair is stuck, ask: 'Where did the strip of width 6 cm come from on the big square?' After the first rectangle is found, ask groups to try different a and b values. Cold-call 3 pairs to read their table rows aloud and write them on the board so everyone can see 84 = 6 × 14 and 56 = 4 × 14. Ask: 'What do you notice about the two lengths of the rectangle and the numbers a and b?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with physical manipulatives and Pattern Finding across Cases. Learners cut and rearrange the shape (SEP 2) and compare a table of examples (SEP 4) to move from specific numbers to a general statement. Moving between the concrete model, the table and the symbols builds a connected understanding that the identity comes from area and is not just a rule to memorise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) are the pieces cut accurately (check measured sides of 6 cm and 14 cm)? (2) can the learner say which side of the rectangle is (a − b) and which is (a + b)? (3) does the second example row in the table match the pattern? (4) can the learner write a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) in their own words? Use a quick checklist on a clipboard. Learners who struggle are given a pre-drawn grid square and asked to shade the L-shape.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners first explain the identity: in pairs, using the diagram, they write why the L-shape area a² − b² equals the rectangle area (a − b)(a + b), noting that the same paper was only rearranged so the area is unchanged. They then compare the three identities side by side: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² and a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). Next they use the identity for mental calculation: 52² − 48² = (52 − 48)(52 + 48) = 4 × 100 = 400, and check against 2704 − 2304 = 400. They try 75² − 25² = 50 × 100 = 5000 and 105² − 95² = 10 × 200 = 2000 (Kericho tea-buying context: 105 kg and 95 kg of tea). Finally, as a preview only, they are shown a 10 by 10 square standing for the largest plot, with a small square of side (x − 10) removed: 100 − (x − 10)² = (10 − (x − 10))(10 + (x − 10)) = (20 − x)(x). They check with x = 8: 100 − 4 = 96 = 8 × 12, and with x = 6: 100 − 16 = 84 = 6 × 14. The full use of this link comes in Lesson 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'In your own words, why does the rectangle have the same area as the L-shape?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for explanations and invite 2 more to add or challenge. Then write the three identities on the board and ask: 'Which one did we find today and which picture matches each one?' Pose: 'Use the shortcut for 52² − 48². Who can show it on the board?' Invite one learner to show the steps and ask the class to confirm with 2704 − 2304. Give a minute for pairs to try 75² − 25² and 105² − 95². Cold-call 2 pairs. Common misconception to raise: 'Is 52² − 48² the same as (52 − 48)²?' Let learners compute 16 versus 400 and discuss. Preview carefully: 'This is just a peek. Take x = 8 on Mama Wanjiru's plot: 100 − (8 − 10)² = 100 − 4 = 96. Do you see 8 × 12 hiding here? We will use it fully in Lesson 8.' Make clear the 8 m and 12 m are the same rectangle turned round.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Contrasting Cases. Learners state the claim (the identity), supply evidence (cut paper and numerical checks), and give reasoning (area is conserved when pieces are rearranged). Contrasting a² − b² with (a − b)² exposes a common error and sharpens understanding. The preview with x = 8 and x = 6 connects the identity to the anchoring phenomenon without pre-empting Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) does the explanation mention that the same pieces were rearranged so area stays the same? (2) can the learner compute 52² − 48² = 400 using the identity and not by squaring? (3) does the learner avoid confusing a² − b² with (a − b)²? (4) can the learner verify 100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x) for x = 8 giving 96? Use mini-whiteboards: each learner shows their answer for 75² − 25² (5000) at the same time and the teacher scans the room.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to the Driving Question Board. They write new questions on sticky notes, for example: 'Does a² − b² work for any numbers, even decimals?', 'Why is the plot area always 100 minus a square?', 'Can we use these identities to work out the widths for a target area?', 'Does a² + b² also factorise?' They also move earlier questions that are now answered, such as 'Why does 8 m give the same area as 12 m?' (partly: the identity suggests symmetry about 10, but the full answer comes in Lesson 6), to a 'Partly answered' column. Each pair places at least one note on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'Today we found a shortcut. What new questions has it raised about Mama Wanjiru's plot?' Give 2 minutes of silent writing and then 2 minutes to post notes. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 3 learners to read their notes aloud and sort them into groups: 'about identities', 'about the plot', 'about solving'. Say: 'Which of these will we answer in the next lessons?' Mark the note about 'a target area without trial and error' with a star and say we will begin working towards it in Lesson 4 with factorising.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Question Sorting. Posting and sorting questions keeps learners as owners of the inquiry and shows that each lesson narrows the gap between the evidence so far and the original puzzle: how to find widths for a target area without trial and error.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) do notes connect to the plot or the identities rather than being random? (2) does at least one question move towards solving for x? (3) can learners say which questions are partly answered? Count the notes per category and record which pairs posted only recall questions so the teacher can prompt them next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class cumulative model on chart paper. The model started in Lesson 2 with area models of squares (version 1). Learners now add a third panel showing the large square with a small square cut from one corner and the rearranged rectangle labelled (a − b) by (a + b). Under the three panels they write the three identities in the exact forms: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² and a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). They add a small link box showing the plot facts: fence 40 m, length = 20 − x, area x(20 − x), 8 m and 12 m both 96 m², 10 m the largest at 100 m², with the note '100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x)? Check in Lesson 8'. Each learner then completes a 3-line summary in their own book.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model has to explain Mama Wanjiru's plot. What did we have before today, and what do we add now?' Invite 3 learners to draw the three panels, with cold-calls for the labels. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after asking 'Which identity belongs under which picture?' Ask: 'What can our model not yet do?' Lead learners to say that it cannot yet find the widths for a target area, so we need to factorise and solve (Lessons 4 to 6). Close with an exit ticket on a half-sheet: 'Use a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) to find 63² − 37², and write one sentence about how it links to a square and the Kericho plot.' (Answer: 26 × 100 = 2600.) Collect the tickets.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Gaps Identified. Adding the third identity to the model shows learners how the evidence is growing from lesson to lesson. Naming what the model still cannot do gives the next lesson a purpose and keeps every phase tied to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators on the exit ticket: (1) correct answer 2600 using (63 − 37)(63 + 37) = 26 × 100; (2) the three identities written correctly in the model; (3) a sentence linking to area of squares or to the plot. Sort tickets into 3 piles (secure, partly secure, not yet). The 'not yet' pile gets a short re-cut of the paper squares at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: 1) Did learners discover the rearrangement themselves, or did they need the cut line suggested? Note which pairs needed support. 2) How many learners still treated a² − b² as (a − b)²? Plan a short mini-lesson with numbers (16 versus 400) if more than a quarter did. 3) Was the preview of 100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x) kept light, so that the full explanation was left for Lesson 8? 4) Did all learners say plainly that widths 8 m and 12 m give the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round? 5) Which mental-calculation example (52² − 48², 75² − 25², 105² − 95²) most engaged learners, and could a local trading context be added next time? 6) Were scissors handled safely and was waste paper collected?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We cut a small square from the corner of a large square and rearranged the L-shape into a rectangle. The rectangle had sides (a − b) and (a + b) and the same area as the L-shape, for example 10 cm and 4 cm gave 6 × 14 = 84 cm². We also saw that 52² − 48² = 4 × 100 = 400 matches 2704 − 2304 = 400, and that for the Kericho plot, x = 8 gives 100 − 4 = 96 = 8 × 12.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The identity a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) is true for all values of a and b. It gives a quick way to calculate differences of squares mentally. Together with (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², it makes up the three identities in our model. The plot area x(20 − x) can be written as 100 − (x − 10)², a preview we will use fully in Lesson 8.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Cutting the L-shape and rearranging the pieces does not change the area, so a² − b² must equal (a − b)(a + b). This helps explain Mama Wanjiru's plot in Kericho: the area is 100 minus a small square, which hints at why widths on either side of 10 m give equal areas (8 m and 12 m are the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round) and why 10 m gives the most, 100 m². We still need to learn how to factorise and solve to find widths for a target area without trial and error.

LESSONS.title: Factorising x² + bx + c: Running the Expansion Backwards to Find the Plot
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; Predict 6 min, Observe 12 min, Explain 10 min, DQB 5 min, Model 7 min)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: factorise; quadratic expression; sum-and-product method; area tiles; x² tile; x strip; unit square; expansion in reverse; (x + p)(x + q); roots; 8 m and 12 m plots; Mama Wanjiru; Kericho; Driving Question Board; cumulative model

slo.purpose: Learners run the expansion (x + p)(x + q) = x² + (p + q)x + pq in reverse. They factorise x² + bx + c by finding two numbers whose sum is b and whose product is c, and check each answer with area tiles or by expanding. They then link x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) back to Mama Wanjiru's 8 m and 12 m plots.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) explain that factorising means writing an expression as a product; (2) state that in x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q), p + q = b and p × q = c; (3) factorise expressions such as x² + 8x + 15 and x² − 20x + 96, including cases where b and c are negative; (4) verify a factorisation by arranging tiles or by expanding; (5) link x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) to the plot widths 8 m and 12 m, which are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round. (KICD Specific Learning Outcome: factorise quadratic expressions.)
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data: look for the pattern between the numbers in an expansion and the coefficients. Using mathematics and computational thinking: list factor pairs of c and test their sums. Developing and using models: build a tile rectangle to represent x² + bx + c. Constructing explanations: justify why the sum and product rule works using the area model. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration; Learning to learn.
slo.attitudes: Values: Responsibility (taking care of shared tile sets and handing them back complete) and Respect (listening to each group member's strategy before correcting). Learners also develop persistence when a factor pair does not work, and appreciation that algebra can unlock real Kenyan farming problems without trial and error. PCIs: Life skills (decision making when choosing between candidate number pairs); Education for Sustainable Development (using locally made cardboard tiles).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? Lesson focus: If we know the area expression x² + bx + c of a rectangle, how can we find its width and length without trial and error?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 showed that the plot area is a quadratic expression and that expanding brackets gives an x² term. Lesson 4 turns the expansion around, which is a key tool for the central puzzle. Here learners discover that x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12), because −8 and −12 have sum −20 and product 96. The numbers 8 and 12 are exactly the two widths that gave 96 m² in the plot table. Lesson 5 extends factorising to ax² + bx + c, and Lesson 6 uses the zero-product property to solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0 properly. This lesson does NOT yet solve the equation formally; it only builds the factorising skill and plants the clue.
slo.safetyNotes: Cardboard tiles have sharp corners, so cut them with blunt-nosed scissors and round off the corners. Keep tiles and string off the floor so no one trips. Collect all tile sets at the end of the lesson and count them back in.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru's children, Chebet and Kiprop, noticed that widths of 8 m and 12 m both enclose 96 m² with her 40 m of wire in Kericho. Today learners find out why those two numbers appear. They predict the dimensions of a rectangle from an area expression, build it with x² tiles, x strips and unit squares, and discover the sum-and-product pattern. They factorise x² + 8x + 15 (from Lesson 1) and then x² − 20x + 96, whose factors (x − 8) and (x − 12) contain the two plot widths. Learners check every answer by expanding. The lesson ends with Driving Question Board (DQB) updates and a revision of the cumulative model, which already holds the area models (Lesson 2) and all three identities (Lesson 3), so that it now records the factorised form of the plot-area equation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of 4. The teacher writes on the board: 'Mama Wanjiru's new bed has area x² + 8x + 15 m². Its width is (x + 3) m. What is its length?' Individually, then in groups, learners write a prediction on a sticky note or in the exercise book: the length, and one sentence explaining how they got it. Some will guess by division, others by recalling the Lesson 1 expansion (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15. Next, learners predict a harder case: 'If the area is x² − 20x + 96, what two brackets multiply to give it? What do you notice about 96 and the plots from the story?' Groups record their prediction and their confidence level (sure, unsure, guessing) for each question. Link to the phenomenon: the 96 m² is the area that both the 8 m and 12 m widths gave.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Mama Wanjiru's plot in Kericho. In Lesson 1 we expanded (x + 3)(x + 5). Today we run it backwards. Before I teach anything, I want your best prediction.' Write the first expression and give 1 minute of silent individual thinking. Then WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking 'What would the missing length be?' before taking any response. Cold-call 3 learners (not volunteers) to share predictions and ask each 'What made you think that?' Do not say whether answers are right. Write the second expression x² − 20x + 96 and ask: 'Where have we seen the number 96 before?' WAIT 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners. Record all predictions on a chart headed 'Our predictions'. Circulate and note which groups use division, trial and error or recall of the expansion.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a confidence rating. Committing to a prediction in writing, together with a confidence level, creates a cognitive stake. When learners later see the tile evidence they notice conflicts between their prediction and the result. Linking 96 to the plot table activates prior knowledge from Lesson 1 and shows that the 8 m and 12 m plots are connected to the expression.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) how many groups write a length of (x + 5) and whether they give a reason; (2) whether learners link the 96 to the 8 m and 12 m plots; (3) whether any learner mentions numbers that add to the middle term and multiply to the last term. Tally on a class checklist: Ready (gives a reason using expansion), Developing (guesses without reason), Needs support (cannot start). Use the tally to form mixed-ability tile groups.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups receive a tile set: 1 x² tile (a square of side x), 10 x strips (x by 1) and 20 unit squares, made from cardboard, with x about 5 cm and 1 unit = 1 cm. Task A (x² + 8x + 15): build a rectangle using exactly 1 x² tile, 8 x strips and 15 unit squares. Learners discover that the x strips split into 3 and 5 and the units form a 3 by 5 block, giving sides (x + 3) and (x + 5). They record the numbers 3 and 5 and fill a table: sum = 8, product = 15. Task B (x² + 7x + 12 and x² + 9x + 20): learners repeat the build and look for the rule. They then list factor pairs of c, test which pair adds to b, and record p, q, p + q and p × q in a table. Task C (negative numbers): the teacher shows a pre-drawn chart of x² − 20x + 96 with the 'minus' tiles drawn in red. Learners list the factor pairs of 96 (1 × 96, 2 × 48, 3 × 32, 4 × 24, 6 × 16, 8 × 12) and test which pair adds to 20. They discover 8 + 12 = 20 and 8 × 12 = 96, so with both negative: −8 + −12 = −20 and (−8)(−12) = 96. Therefore x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12). Learners then expand (x − 8)(x − 12) to confirm: x² − 12x − 8x + 96 = x² − 20x + 96. Finally, learners notice that 8 and 12 are the same widths that gave 96 m² in the plot table.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute tile sets with the instruction: 'Take care of these tiles; they belong to the whole class. Count them before and after.' Say: 'Build x² + 8x + 15 as a single rectangle. No gaps, no overlaps. Then tell me the two side lengths.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Where are your 8 strips? How did you split them?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before any hint. Cold-call 2 groups to show their tile rectangle to the class. Give the table prompt: 'What do you notice about the numbers on the sides, 3 and 5, and the numbers in the expression, 8 and 15?' WAIT 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. For Task C say: 'Mama Wanjiru's children found 8 m and 12 m both give 96. List all the factor pairs of 96. Which pair adds to 20?' Support learners who confuse signs by asking: 'If the product is positive and the sum is negative, what must be true about both numbers?' Ask groups to expand their answer as a check before moving on. Watch for learners who find pairs with the right product but ignore the sum.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) with Pattern Finding. Learners first use physical tiles (concrete), then complete a table of p, q, sum and product (representational), then state the rule in symbols (abstract). Because they run Lesson 1's expansion in reverse, they see that the rule p + q = b and p × q = c is the same pattern read backwards. Pattern finding in a table lets learners generate the rule themselves rather than being told it.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learner builds a closed rectangle with no gaps and names both sides; (2) the table has correct p, q, sum and product values for at least two expressions; (3) learner lists factor pairs of 96 systematically and identifies 8 and 12; (4) learner expands (x − 8)(x − 12) correctly to verify. Use a quick check: ask each group to show a mini-whiteboard with the factorisation of x² + 9x + 20. Note groups that show (x + 4)(x + 5) as ready and those with wrong signs or swapped values as needing a prompt.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their groups to write a short 'Factorising Recipe' using their evidence: Step 1: look at c and list pairs of numbers that multiply to c. Step 2: choose the pair that adds to b. Step 3: write (x + p)(x + q). Step 4: check by expanding. They then apply the recipe to new expressions on a worksheet: x² + 10x + 21, x² + 6x + 8, x² − 9x + 20, x² − 7x + 10 and x² + 2x − 15. For x² + 2x − 15, learners must work out that one number is negative: 5 and −3 give sum 2 and product −15, so (x + 5)(x − 3). Each learner explains to a partner why the signs behave as they do. Finally, each group answers in writing: 'How does factorising x² − 20x + 96 as (x − 8)(x − 12) help explain why the 8 m and 12 m plots have the same area?' Expected idea: the numbers 8 and 12 add up to 20, which is the fence half-length, so a width of 8 m gives a length of 12 m and a width of 12 m gives a length of 8 m. These are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round, not two different shapes. Learners should recognise that the factors give the two widths but are not asked to solve the equation formally yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your tile evidence to write the recipe in your own words. Which step would you teach a Grade 9 learner first?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after posing 'Why must both numbers be negative when the sum is negative and the product is positive?' Cold-call 3 learners to answer, then ask a fourth to restate. For x² + 2x − 15 ask: 'What is different about the product here? What does that tell you about the signs of p and q?' Cold-call 2 pairs to share. State plainly: 'The plots with widths 8 m and 12 m are the SAME rectangle turned round. Their widths add up to 20 m, half of the 40 m of wire.' Do not formally solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0 or introduce the zero-product property; say: 'In Lesson 6 we will use these brackets to solve the equation. Today we only factorise.' Address the misconception that (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 15 by asking the learner to expand it with tiles. Collect 3 worksheets to check accuracy before the lesson ends.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Self-Explanation and Peer Teaching (Turn-and-Talk). Writing a recipe in their own words forces learners to organise the procedure and the reason behind it. Explaining signs to a partner exposes gaps in reasoning. Connecting the factorisation back to 8 m and 12 m moves the lesson from a procedure to an explanation of the phenomenon: the numbers in the brackets are the plot widths that give 96 m².
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the recipe includes both the sum and product conditions and a check step; (2) learner correctly factorises at least 4 of 5 expressions, including at least one with a negative c; (3) in their written answer learners state that 8 + 12 = 20 and 8 × 12 = 96, and that the 8 m and 12 m plots are the same rectangle turned round; (4) no learner claims the two plots are different shapes. Collect exit slips with the factorisation of x² − 11x + 24 (answer (x − 3)(x − 8)). Sort slips into Secure, Nearly and Not yet for the next lesson's grouping.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the main question: 'How can we use quadratic expressions and equations to find the dimensions of a plot when its fence length and area are both fixed, and why do two different plots sometimes have the same area?' Each group writes on sticky notes (a) one thing they can now answer, for example 'How do we find the two numbers in the brackets?' and (b) one new question, for example 'Can we use the brackets to find the width directly?', 'What if the number in front of x² is not 1?' or 'Does every expression factorise?'. They place answered notes under 'Answered so far' with the evidence (the tile picture or the sum-and-product table) and new questions under 'Still wondering'. The class sorts the notes into themes such as 'Solving the equation' (Lesson 6) and 'Harder expressions' (Lesson 5).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our DQB. Which question can we now answer with the evidence from our tiles?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to place one note each and justify it with evidence. Ask: 'What new question has factorising raised about Mama Wanjiru's plot?' Cold-call 2 learners. Point out the key unanswered question: 'We found brackets with 8 and 12 in them. How do we know that x = 8 and x = 12 are the widths? That is the job of Lesson 6.' Group related notes with a marker and label themes. Do not answer new questions now; promise when they will be addressed (Lesson 5: ax² + bx + c; Lesson 6: solving the equation).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question Clustering on the Driving Question Board. Sorting questions into 'answered' and 'still wondering' makes progress visible and gives learners ownership of the learning path. Each answered note must cite evidence, so learners practise linking claims to data. New questions drive the sequence into Lessons 5 and 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least one answered note per group cites tile or table evidence; (2) new questions are productive (about solving, about a not equal to 1, or about the maximum) rather than off-topic; (3) learners can say which lesson will likely answer their question. Record the number of groups that ask a question about turning the brackets into widths, as a sign that they are ready for Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their cumulative model of Mama Wanjiru's plot, which contains the v1 area models (Lesson 2) and all three identities (Lesson 3). In groups, they add a new section called 'Factorised form'. They copy the new relationship for the plot: Area = x(20 − x) = 20x − x²; target 96 m²: x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12), because −8 + −12 = −20 and (−8)(−12) = 96. They draw a simple diagram showing the 8 m by 12 m rectangle in two orientations, labelled 'width 8 m, length 12 m' and 'width 12 m, length 8 m', with a note: 'the same rectangle turned round; width + length = 20 m'. They also add the sum-and-product rule in a box: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) where p + q = b and p × q = c, with the check 'expand to confirm'. Finally, each learner writes one sentence on what the model can now explain and one thing it cannot yet do (it cannot yet show that x = 8 and x = 12 are the solutions; it does not yet explain the maximum area of 100 m²).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model has area models and three identities. What new idea from today must go in?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to suggest additions. Check that the diagram shows 8 m by 12 m as ONE rectangle turned round, and that the widths add to 20 m. Ask: 'Why do the numbers 8 and 12 add to 20 in our model?' Cold-call 2 learners. Challenge: 'Our model shows factors of x² − 20x + 96. Does it yet tell us the solutions? What is still missing?' Accept 'zero-product property' only as a hint at Lesson 6; do not teach it. Give each learner a 2-question exit task: factorise x² + 12x + 35 and x² − 13x + 36, then check one by expanding. Collect the tasks. Remind learners to return all tiles.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision. Learners revise a shared model rather than start a new one, which shows how each lesson adds a tool for explaining the phenomenon. Stating what the model can and cannot yet explain builds scientific habits of mind: models are improved by evidence and have limits. It also sets up Lesson 6, where the factorised form will be used to solve the equation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the revised model contains x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) with the correct sum −20 and product 96; (2) the diagram shows ONE 8 m by 12 m rectangle in two orientations; (3) learner names a limit (cannot yet solve for x or explain the maximum); (4) exit task: x² + 12x + 35 = (x + 5)(x + 7) and x² − 13x + 36 = (x − 4)(x − 9), with a correct expansion check for at least one. Learners who get both correct are Secure; those with sign errors get a short tile re-teach at the start of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners discover the sum-and-product rule from the tile patterns, or did I tell it too early? (2) Which learners listed factor pairs systematically, and which guessed? (3) Did any learners say the 8 m and 12 m plots are two different shapes, and how did I correct this? (4) How well did learners handle negative numbers, especially in x² + 2x − 15? (5) Did the link between (x − 8)(x − 12) and the plot widths feel meaningful, or did it seem like a coincidence? (6) Did I resist solving the equation formally, leaving it for Lesson 6? (7) Did tile shortages or sharing problems affect the activity, and could locally made cardboard tiles help? (8) Which exit-slip errors will shape the opening of Lesson 5?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built rectangles from x² tiles, x strips and unit squares. x² + 8x + 15 made a rectangle with sides (x + 3) and (x + 5). For x² − 20x + 96 we listed the factor pairs of 96 and found that 8 × 12 = 96 and 8 + 12 = 20.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers p and q whose sum is b and whose product is c, then write (x + p)(x + q). Check by expanding. When the sum is negative and the product is positive, both numbers are negative.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) because −8 + −12 = −20 and (−8)(−12) = 96. The numbers 8 and 12 are the widths that gave 96 m² on Mama Wanjiru's 40 m fence in Kericho. They add up to 20 m, so the 8 m and 12 m plots are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round.
