LESSONS.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 1) and Special Cases: Which Method Works Best?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: factorise, grouping method, area-tile method, ax² + bx + c, perfect square, difference of two squares, check by expansion, Kericho plot

slo.purpose: Learners factorise ax² + bx + c where a ≠ 1 so that they can later solve target-area equations for Mama Wanjiru's 40 m fenced plot when the area expression has a number in front of x².
slo.knowledge: Learners factorise ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 1) using the grouping method (split the middle term using two numbers whose product is ac and whose sum is b) and the area-tile method. They recognise x² + 10x + 25 as a perfect square (a + b)² and x² − 100 as a difference of two squares (a − b)(a + b), and they check every answer by expansion. KICD strand outcome: the learner should be able to factorise quadratic expressions.
slo.skills: Splitting the middle term, grouping and taking out common factors, arranging area tiles into a rectangle, checking by expansion, comparing methods and justifying a choice, and communicating reasoning. NGSS-style practices: Developing and Using Models (tile and area models), Analysing and Interpreting Data (comparing methods), and Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Precision and integrity in checking work, perseverance when the first split fails, and respect for classmates' different methods. KICD values: Responsibility and Unity. KICD core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, and Communication and Collaboration. PCI: Life Skills (decision making).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? (Lesson focus: How do we factorise when the x² term has a number in front, and which method should we choose?) (The KICD key inquiry wording is to be verified against the KICD page.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 gave the sum-and-product method for x² + bx + c. Real plots with extra rules often give an x² term with a number in front, so this lesson extends factorising to a ≠ 1. It also links the special cases from Lessons 2 and 3 and holds a DQB review of which methods work best. Lesson 6 will use this factorising to solve equations such as x² − 20x + 96 = 0, which resolves the central puzzle.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use only paper tiles, grid paper, scissors and string loops. Scissors are used with care and the cutting is done at desks. Keep bags and string off the floor to avoid tripping. No hazardous materials are used.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru's children, Chebet and Kiprop, know that her 40 m of wire gives the area x(20 − x), and in Lesson 4 the class factorised x² + bx + c using sum and product. Now the class asks what to do when there is a number in front of x², such as 2x² + 7x + 3. Learners predict how many rectangles of tiles can be built, then build 2x² + 7x + 3 from area tiles (two x² tiles, seven x strips, three unit squares) and find the rectangle (2x + 1) by (x + 3). They then use the grouping method (ac = 6, split 6x and x: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3)) and check by expansion. Learners test the special cases x² + 10x + 25 (a perfect square) and x² − 100 (a difference of two squares, from Lessons 2 and 3). Finally the class reviews the Driving Question Board (DQB) to decide which method works best and when, and revises the cumulative model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Mama Wanjiru's plot from Kericho: 40 m of wire, width x m, length (20 − x) m. The teacher writes 2x² + 7x + 3 on the board and says that Chebet found a plot-style rectangle with this area. Individually, then in pairs, learners predict on their sheets: (1) Can sum and product from Lesson 4 factorise this directly? (2) What might the two sides of the rectangle look like? They write a first guess such as (2x + 3)(x + 1) and keep it to test later.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "Mama Wanjiru's area x(20 − x) has an x² term. What if the x² term has a number in front, like 2x²?" Write 2x² + 7x + 3 on the board. Say: "Write your prediction silently first." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then 2 minutes of silent writing. Pair-share for 1 minute. Cold-call 4 learners to give a guess for the two brackets, writing every guess on the board without saying which is right. Ask: "What would you do to check a guess?" and take the answer "expand it".
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction phase): committing to a guess before instruction makes learners notice the gap in Lesson 4's method, so they have a reason to learn a new method, and wrong guesses become evidence to compare later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) at least 10 of 12 sampled learners write a prediction instead of leaving the sheet blank; (b) learners who propose expanding to check show they remember Lesson 1 expansion; (c) the teacher notes on a tally how many guesses are of the form (2x + p)(x + q), (x + p)(x + q) or no guess. Learners who write (x + 3)(x + 1) show they have not noticed the 2 in front of x².

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (area tiles, about 8 minutes): in groups of 4, learners use cut paper tiles (an x² tile, an x strip, a unit square) to build 2x² + 7x + 3 using 2 x² tiles, 7 x strips and 3 unit squares. They must arrange all tiles into one rectangle with no gaps and read the sides. They find the rectangle with sides (2x + 1) and (x + 3). They sketch it on grid paper. Part B (grouping, about 8 minutes): the teacher guides them to find ac = 2 × 3 = 6 and two numbers with product 6 and sum 7 (6 and 1). They split the middle term: 2x² + 6x + x + 3, group as (2x² + 6x) + (x + 3), take out common factors 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) and get (2x + 1)(x + 3). They check by expansion: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x² + 7x + 3. They then compare with their tile picture: the 6x + x strips are the two x-strip groups on the sides of the rectangle. Part C (special cases, about 5 minutes): learners test x² + 10x + 25 by tiles and by sum and product (5 and 5): (x + 5)² and link it to (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² from Lesson 2. They test x² − 100 with a missing middle term: (x − 10)(x + 10), linking to a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) from Lesson 3.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Say: "Use all the pieces. No gaps, no overlaps. Read the length and width of your rectangle." Ask groups: "Where is the x² part of your rectangle? Where are the 7 strips?" For grouping, write 2x² + 7x + 3 on the board and ask: "What is a × c? Which two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 7?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before cold-calling 3 learners for the pair of numbers. Ask: "Why must we split 7x into 6x and x, not 5x and 2x?" (5x + 2x also adds to 7x but the grouping will not give a common bracket.) Have learners try 5 and 2 and see that the brackets do not match. Insist everyone checks by expansion. For the special cases, ask: "Which of these has no middle term? What does Lesson 3 tell us?" Cold-call 3 learners to explain.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with multiple representations: the same factorisation is shown as a tile rectangle, a grouping calculation and an expansion check. Matching the pieces across all three connects the algebra to the area of Mama Wanjiru's plot, so factorising is seen as finding the sides of a rectangle from its area.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) groups form a complete rectangle with sides (2x + 1) and (x + 3) within 8 minutes; (b) learners write ac = 6 correctly and name 6 and 1; (c) learners show the check by expansion on paper; (d) learners recognise x² + 10x + 25 as (x + 5)² and x² − 100 as (x − 10)(x + 10). Watch for a common error: leaving out the second group's factor of 1 and writing 2x(x + 3) + (x + 3) wrongly as 2x(x + 3). Prompt: "What is left when you take out (x + 3) from x + 3?"

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs on three new expressions: (1) 3x² + 10x + 3 (ac = 9, numbers 9 and 1, giving (3x + 1)(x + 3)); (2) 2x² + 5x + 2 (ac = 4, numbers 4 and 1, giving (2x + 1)(x + 2)); (3) x² + 6x + 9 and 4x² − 25 as special cases, giving (x + 3)² and (2x − 5)(2x + 5). Each pair factorises one expression by the area-tile or grouping method and one by the other method, and checks every answer by expansion. Then each pair writes a 'Method Card' explaining in two sentences when each method is useful. Finally they connect back to the phenomenon: x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) from Lesson 4 can be done by sum and product (−8 and −12 add to −20, multiply to 96), and the class discusses whether grouping gives the same answer (split −20x as −8x − 12x).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Choose a different method for each of your two expressions. Explain to your partner why you chose it." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 5 pairs in total, one for each expression and one for the Method Card. Ask: "How did you know your answer was right?" and expect "we expanded". Ask: "Is (x + 3)² the same as x² + 9? Show me with your tiles." Use the error to reinforce Lesson 2. For the phenomenon link, ask: "Mama Wanjiru's 96 m² equation was x² − 20x + 96. Does grouping give the same brackets as sum and product?" Support learners who struggle by giving a half-completed grouping frame. Extension: ask fast groups to factorise 6x² + 11x + 3 (ac = 18, numbers 9 and 2, giving (2x + 3)(3x + 1)).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Peer explanation and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: each pair states a claim (the factorised form), supplies evidence (expansion or tile picture) and gives reasoning (why the chosen method fitted). Explaining why a method was chosen builds strategic understanding and not only procedure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) at least 8 of 12 sampled pairs correctly factorise at least two of the three expressions; (b) every answer carries a visible expansion check; (c) the Method Card gives a reason such as "no middle term means difference of two squares" or "a = 1 means sum and product"; (d) learners say that factorising x² − 20x + 96 gives the 8 and 12 of the plot widths. Learners who cannot split the middle term receive the prompt "Which two numbers multiply to ac and add to b?" and a short list of factor pairs.

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the Driving Question Board. Learners review the questions already posted, for example "Why do 8 m and 12 m give the same area?" and "How do we find widths without trial and error?" They add sticky notes with new questions or partial answers from today, such as "Which method works best, and when?" and "Can every quadratic be factorised?" Groups sort the methods into a table on the board: sum and product (a = 1), grouping (a ≠ 1), area tiles (any, but helpful for seeing why), and the special cases (perfect square, difference of two squares). They place a sticky note on questions that today's lesson helped to answer, and mark the question "How do we find the widths for a target area?" as 'closer, needs solving in Lesson 6'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board. Which questions did factorising help us with today? Which questions are still open?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to move or add a note and explain why. Ask: "Which method would you choose for x² + 14x + 49? For 5x² − 20? For 3x² + 8x + 4? Why?" Take a quick show of hands for each choice and ask 2 learners to defend theirs. Record the class's agreed rules of thumb: first look for a common factor or special case, then use sum and product if a = 1, otherwise use grouping, and use tiles to see or check. Say: "Next lesson we will use these factors to actually find the widths."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board review: sorting questions into answered, partly answered and open shows learners their growing understanding and keeps the Kericho plot problem as the purpose for each new skill. Comparing methods builds the habit of choosing a strategy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) each group adds at least one new question or partial answer; (b) learners justify a method choice with a feature of the expression (for example, "no middle term"); (c) learners identify 'solve (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0' as the next step without prompting; (d) the teacher records which questions learners think are still open. If fewer than half can justify their choice, repeat the choice task with two more expressions at the start of Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the cumulative class model. In their notebooks they add a new section to the model: 'Factorising turns an area into its sides.' They draw the 2x² + 7x + 3 tile rectangle with sides (2x + 1) and (x + 3), write the grouping steps beside it, and add a flow chart: 'Look for a special case or common factor → if a = 1 use sum and product → if a ≠ 1 use grouping or tiles → check by expansion.' They add a link to the phenomenon: x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12), where 8 and 12 are the plot widths that give 96 m² with the 40 m fence, and the 8 m and 12 m plots are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round. They write one sentence on what is still missing: "We have not yet used the factors to find x."
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Add today's idea to our model. How does factorising help us find the sides of Mama Wanjiru's plot?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners for their sentence. Check that learners state plainly that widths 8 m and 12 m describe the same rectangle turned round and not two different shapes. Ask: "If (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, what might x be?" Take guesses but do not confirm, saying "We will prove it in Lesson 6." Collect the notebooks of 6 learners to check the flow chart and the expansion checks. Assign a short practice: factorise 2x² + 5x + 3 and x² + 12x + 36, and check both by expansion.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding factorising to the earlier area models and identities shows how the pieces fit together, and the 'still missing' sentence keeps the next step (solving) connected to the central puzzle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) the model includes the tile rectangle, the grouping steps and the expansion check; (b) the flow chart puts 'check special cases first' and 'check by expansion' in sensible places; (c) learners write that factorising gives the sides of the plot from its area; (d) the practice answers (2x + 3)(x + 1) and (x + 6)² are correct. A learner who writes (x + 6)² = x² + 36 needs to revisit Lesson 2 with tiles.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, check: Which learners could split the middle term without the tiles, and which relied on the tiles? How many learners checked by expansion without being reminded? Did anyone confuse (x + 5)² with x² + 25? Was the 8 m and 12 m plot explained as one rectangle turned round and not two shapes? Which method did learners prefer and did their reasons match the expression? What would you change in the grouping instruction or the Method Card task? Note any learners who need extra practice on factor pairs before Lesson 6, where factorising is used to solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built 2x² + 7x + 3 from area tiles (two x² tiles, seven x strips, three unit squares) and found a rectangle with sides (2x + 1) and (x + 3). We also saw that x² + 10x + 25 makes a square and that x² − 100 has no middle term.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: To factorise ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 1, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term, group, take out common factors, and check by expansion. Perfect squares and differences of two squares are special cases to look for first.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Factorising turns an area back into the sides of a rectangle, just as x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) gives the widths 8 m and 12 m for Mama Wanjiru's 96 m² plot. Which method is best depends on the expression: a special case, sum and product when a = 1, or grouping or tiles when a ≠ 1. We still need to use the factors to find x, which is the next lesson.

LESSONS.title: Two Widths, One Area: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; the KICD lesson allocation for this sub-strand should be verified against the KICD page)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: quadratic equation, zero-product property, factorisation, root, solution, standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, check against context, Mama Wanjiru's plot, Kericho

slo.purpose: Learners use the zero-product property to solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0 after factorising it, and interpret both solutions in the plot context. This resolves the central puzzle of the phenomenon: why widths 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m².
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (1) a quadratic equation is a quadratic expression set equal to 0, written in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0; (2) the zero-product property says if p × q = 0 then p = 0 or q = 0; (3) x(20 − x) = 96 rearranges to x² − 20x + 96 = 0, which factorises as (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, so x = 8 or x = 12; (4) the two solutions describe the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round, because width + length = 20 m; (5) solutions must be checked against the context 0 < x < 20.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: rearrange an equation to zero, factorise it using the sum-and-product method from Lessons 4 and 5, apply the zero-product property to find both roots, check each root by substituting into x(20 − x), and explain in words what each root means for Mama Wanjiru's plot. NGSS-style practices embedded: Analysing and Interpreting Data (comparing the area table with the roots), Constructing Explanations (why two roots), Developing and Using Models (revising the cumulative model).
slo.attitudes: Learners show perseverance when a product is not 0, curiosity about why two answers appear, and respect for peers' reasoning in pair discussions. Values: Responsibility (checking answers carefully), Unity (sharing methods in pairs). Core competencies: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Communication and Collaboration. Kenyan PCI: Life Skills (decision making in planning land use). KICD wording for outcomes, competencies, values and PCIs for this sub-strand must be copied verbatim from the KICD page when finalising, as the supplied OCR text does not contain this sub-strand.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions (verify wording against the KICD page): 1. How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? 2. Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? Lesson focus question: How can we solve x(20 − x) = 96 without trial and error, and why do two widths appear?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 5 built the area expression x(20 − x) = 20x − x², the area models, the identities and factorising skills. In Lesson 6 learners turn the target-area question into an equation and solve it. This resolves the central puzzle of the phenomenon (8 m and 12 m both give 96 m²) and revises the cumulative model to include two solutions. Lesson 7 will extend this to other real-life situations and rejecting invalid solutions, and Lesson 8 to design tasks and the maximum area.
slo.safetyNotes: Low-risk classroom lesson. Use blunt-tipped scissors for any paper cut-outs and keep string loops and tiles off the floor to prevent tripping. Ensure bags are stored away from walkways. Be sensitive that some learners may find it hard to publicly state wrong answers; use pair-sharing first.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru in Kericho has exactly 40 m of wire for a rectangular vegetable plot of sukuma wiki and spinach, so width x m means length (20 − x) m and area x(20 − x). Her children Chebet and Kiprop found that widths 8 m and 12 m both give 96 m². Until now learners found this by trial and error from the area table. In this lesson they predict how many widths could give 96 m², observe how the equation x(20 − x) = 96 becomes x² − 20x + 96 = 0, factorise it to (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0 and use the zero-product property to get x = 8 or x = 12. They explain that both answers are the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round (width and length add up to 20 m), check both against the context, add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise the cumulative model to include two solutions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in pairs with the area table from Lesson 1 hidden except for the row x = 10, A = 100. On a half-sheet they individually write: (a) how many different widths could give exactly 96 m² with the 40 m fence, and why; (b) a guess for each width. They then write one sentence on whether there could be a way to find the widths without trying numbers. Pairs share and write their prediction on a sticky note labelled 'My prediction about Mama Wanjiru's plot'.
framework.teacherMoves: Display: 'Mama Wanjiru wants the plot to enclose exactly 96 m² using all 40 m of wire. Chebet says one width works. Kiprop says two widths work. Who do you think is right?' Say: 'Write your own answer first. Do not talk yet.' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds before pairs speak, then 2 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and compare for one minute.' Cold-call 4 pairs: 'Chebet's way or Kiprop's way, and what is your reason?' Record all predictions on the board in two columns (one width / two widths) without saying who is correct. Say: 'Hold on to your prediction, today we will test it with mathematics, not guessing.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revisit: committing to a prediction in writing creates a cognitive stake, so learners pay attention to the evidence and notice when their thinking changes. Learners' reasons (e.g. 'the table goes up then down') reveal prior ideas about symmetry that can be built on in the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: do learners reason from the area table pattern (rising then falling) or from guesses? Listen for the idea that 'the areas go up and come down' as evidence of symmetry. Count how many pairs predict two widths and note how many give a reason. Success indicator: at least 3 of the 4 cold-called pairs give a reason that refers to the table or to the sum width + length = 20 m.

framework.learnerExperience: Step 1: Learners write the area equation: x(20 − x) = 96. In pairs they expand the bracket (Lesson 1) and rearrange to standard form, getting 20x − x² = 96, so x² − 20x + 96 = 0. Step 2: Learners recall factorising (Lessons 4 and 5) and find two numbers whose sum is −20 and whose product is 96 (−8 and −12), writing (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0. They check by expanding. Step 3: With a teacher demonstration using strips, learners observe the zero-product property: they are given 'Mystery product cards' where p × q = 0 (e.g. 7 × ? = 0, ? × ? = 0 with one factor 0) and list what must be true. They then apply it: x − 8 = 0 or x − 12 = 0, so x = 8 or x = 12. Step 4: Learners substitute both values into x(20 − x): 8 × 12 = 96 and 12 × 8 = 96. They test a non-root, x = 9, in (x − 8)(x − 12) = 1 × (−3) = −3 ≠ 0, to see that the product is zero only at the roots. They record all in an observation table: step, working, what it shows.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out the observation table and mystery product cards. Say: 'We have a target area of 96 m². Last time we guessed from a table. Today we will use an equation.' Ask: 'What is the length when the width is x?' and cold-call 2 learners (20 − x). Write x(20 − x) = 96 and ask: 'What must I do to get everything on one side equal to zero?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for each step of rearranging. For factorising say: 'Use the sum-and-product method from Lesson 4: which two numbers multiply to give 96 and add to give −20?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds, then pairs list factor pairs of 96 on mini-whiteboards. Check by expanding (x − 8)(x − 12) with 2 volunteers. For zero-product, hold up the card '__ × __ = 0' and ask: 'If two numbers multiply to give 0, what can you say about at least one of them?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'Why can't we say the same for a product equal to 96? For example, if p × q = 96, does p have to be 8?' Walk around and ask 'How do you know it works?' Prompt substitution: 'Put x = 8 and then x = 12 into x(20 − x). What do you get?' Also test x = 9: 'Is (x − 8)(x − 12) zero?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Observation table with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: each row records what was done (claim), the working (evidence) and why it is allowed (reasoning, e.g. 'zero-product property'). Contrasting product = 0 with product = 96 helps learners see why we rearrange to zero before splitting into factors, building the key idea instead of a memorised rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check mini-whiteboards: 100% of pairs should write x² − 20x + 96 = 0 correctly. Look for the common error of writing (x + 8)(x + 12) (sign error) or stopping at (x − 8)(x − 12) = 96. Success indicators: learners correct sign errors after the expansion check, at least 80% explain 'one of the brackets must be zero', and learners state that they rearranged to zero first. Record the names of learners who need a Lesson 4 re-teach card.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 3 to produce a short written explanation answering three prompts: (1) Why does the equation give two answers? (2) What do x = 8 and x = 12 mean for the plot? (3) Are they two different shapes? They draw both plots on grid paper using the 40 cm string loop (1 cm = 1 m): one with width 8 cm and length 12 cm, the other with width 12 cm and length 8 cm, and turn one around to see that they are the same rectangle. They compare with 4 m by 24 m (area 96 m² but needs 56 m of wire) to see why only x and 20 − x pair up with a fixed fence. They check the context rule 0 < x < 20 for both roots. They also link back to the area table (rows x = 8 and x = 12, both 96) and note that the roots add up to 20.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Chebet and Kiprop said two different plots give the same area. Use today's mathematics to settle it.' Give groups 5 minutes with the string loops and grid paper. Circulate and ask: 'What is the length when the width is 8? When the width is 12?' and 'What do you notice about the two roots and the number 20?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds after each question. Then hold a whole-class talk: cold-call 3 groups in turn: 'Is it one plot or two plots?' and press: 'Say it in terms of width and length.' Make sure the language is plain: 'The 8 m by 12 m plot turned round is the same rectangle.' Ask: 'Why do the roots add up to 20?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners (width + length = 20, so if x is a width the other root is the length). Show 4 m by 24 m on the board: 'It also has area 96 m², so why is it not on Mama Wanjiru's list?' (Cold-call 2: it needs 56 m of wire, not 40 m.) Finally ask: 'Should we accept every root?' and have learners confirm 8 and 12 both lie between 0 and 20.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model-based explanation with physical turning of the string-loop rectangle: manipulating the concrete model resolves the conflict between 'two answers' and 'one plot', and connects the abstract roots to the symmetry seen in the area table. Group talk using sentence frames ('The roots are 8 and 12 because ... This means the plot ...') supports precise mathematical language.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 1-minute exit explanation on a slip: 'Explain in two sentences why x = 8 and x = 12 are not two different plots.' Success indicator: the learner states that the 8 m by 12 m plot is the same rectangle with width and length swapped, and that width + length = 20 m. Look for the misconception that 'two answers means two different shapes'. At least 75% of slips should include the 'turned round' idea; re-address with the string loop for those who do not.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. In pairs they sort the existing question cards into 'now answered' and 'still open'. They answer the question 'Why do two different widths give the same area?' with an evidence card citing the roots 8 and 12 and the string-loop rectangle. Each learner writes at least one new question on a card, for example: 'What if the target area is 100 m²?', 'What if the target is 105 m²?', 'Does every quadratic equation have two roots?', 'Why is the maximum 100 m²?', 'What if the equation will not factorise?'. Learners place cards on the board under headings: Solving, Context checks, Maximum area, Other situations.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we cross off or answer now, and what is your evidence?' Cold-call 3 learners to move a question card and read the evidence aloud. WAIT TIME 10 seconds before each cold-call. Say: 'Now write one new question that today's results make you wonder about.' Give 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 learners to read new questions and pose a follow-up: 'Which lesson do you think will help answer this?' Point out that the question about 100 m² and 105 m² will come back in later lessons and that other situations such as a mandazi tray and a thrown ball come next. Do not answer these new questions yet; record them as 'to be investigated'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: making the growth in understanding visible lets learners track what evidence resolved a question and turns remaining uncertainty into purposeful inquiry for the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the new question cards. Strong questions extend the phenomenon (e.g. what happens at x = 10, what if the target is above 100) rather than repeat what was learned. Success indicator: at least 80% of learners write one new question that links to the fence, the area or the number of roots, and 3 or more pairs can cite specific evidence (the factorised equation or the string-loop rectangle) for a card they moved.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class cumulative model of Mama Wanjiru's plot. The model currently holds the area models (Lesson 2) and all three identities (Lesson 3). In groups of 4 they add a new panel titled 'Solving for a target area': (1) A = x(20 − x) = 20x − x² (from Lesson 1), (2) target equation x(20 − x) = 96 becoming x² − 20x + 96 = 0, (3) factorised form (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, (4) zero-product property giving x = 8 or x = 12, (5) a sketch showing the 8 m by 12 m rectangle and the same rectangle turned round, and (6) a note: width + length = 20, so the two solutions are x and 20 − x. They mark 'Model v2: two solutions'. Learners add an arrow labelled 'Still to explain: maximum area' and one 'check against the context 0 < x < 20' tick box.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now explain why two widths give 96 m². What new part must we add?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups for a proposal, then agree on the panel. Circulate and ask each group: 'Show me where the model says why there are two answers.' and 'Where does the 20 m come in?' Ask one group to present and cold-call 2 other groups to challenge: 'What is missing or unclear?' Ask: 'What would the model predict for a target of 84 m²?' (Cold-call 2: x² − 20x + 84 = 0 gives 6 and 14; do not solve fully, as this is Lesson 8 content, just have them predict that two widths appear and add to 20.) Close with: 'Which of your predictions at the start was right, and what changed in your thinking?' Cold-call 3 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners integrate new evidence into a shared representation, test it with a new prediction and identify gaps. This makes explicit the link between algebra (roots), geometry (rectangle turned round) and context (fence length), and reveals what the model still cannot explain (maximum area).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group's panel for: correct equation chain, both roots, the 'turned round' sketch, and the note that the roots add to 20. Success indicators: all groups include both solutions and link them to the same rectangle; at least 3 groups can predict that a different target area would again give two widths summing to 20. Collect an exit ticket: 'Solve x² − 20x + 96 = 0 and say what the answers mean for Mama Wanjiru.' At least 80% should score full marks.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask: Did learners see why we rearrange to zero before using the zero-product property, or did they treat it as a rule? Which learners still made sign errors when factorising x² − 20x + 96, and do they need a Lesson 4 refresher with tiles? How many learners explained the two roots as the same rectangle turned round rather than two shapes? Which new DQB questions most strongly point to Lessons 7 and 8 (other situations, maximum area, impossible targets)? What would you change about the wait times or cold-call counts so quieter learners participate?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We saw that x(20 − x) = 96 can be rearranged to x² − 20x + 96 = 0 and factorised as (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0. Substituting x = 8 and x = 12 into x(20 − x) both gave 96 m², while x = 9 did not make the product zero.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a quadratic equation is solved by rearranging to zero, factorising and using the zero-product property: if p × q = 0 then p = 0 or q = 0. We also learned to check each solution against the context 0 < x < 20.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The two solutions x = 8 and x = 12 appear because width + length = 20 m, so if the width is 8 m the length is 12 m and vice versa. They describe the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round, not two different shapes, which resolves the puzzle in Mama Wanjiru's plot. Our model now includes two solutions that add up to 20.

LESSONS.title: Forming and Solving Quadratic Equations from Real-Life Situations: Mandazi Tray, Path Around the Shamba and Thrown Ball
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; double lesson recommended if the ball activity is done outdoors)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: quadratic equation, define the variable, form an equation, rearrange to zero, factorise, zero-product property, root, reject invalid solution, context check, mandazi tray, path, thrown ball, Mama Wanjiru's plot

slo.purpose: Learners translate three worded situations (mandazi tray, path around a shamba, thrown ball) into quadratic equations by defining a variable, writing the equation and rearranging to zero. They solve by factorisation and decide which solutions fit the context. This extends the driving question: the same steps that found the 8 m and 12 m widths for Mama Wanjiru's plot work for many real situations.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to form quadratic equations from real-life situations (KICD sub-strand outcome: form, solve and apply quadratic equations in real-life situations). Learners will know that: (1) a word problem becomes an equation once the unknown is defined with a letter and units; (2) the equation is rearranged to the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 before factorising; (3) the zero-product property gives up to two roots; (4) each root must be checked against the context, so a negative length or width is rejected, while in the ball situation both t = 1 s and t = 3 s are valid.
slo.skills: NGSS-aligned practices: Developing and using models (draw the tray, path and ball path to represent the situation); Using mathematics and computational thinking (form, rearrange, factorise and solve); Analysing and interpreting data (check roots against the context and an area or height table); Constructing explanations (justify why a root is kept or rejected); Engaging in argument from evidence (defend choices in a gallery walk). Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: checking every answer honestly, even when it looks neat. Responsibility: using the fence-wire, grid paper and string models with care. Unity: sharing roles in groups. Appreciation of how mathematics supports decisions for farmers, traders and athletes in Kenya. PCI link: Life skills (decision making) as learners decide which answers make sense.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations? (KICD key inquiry questions; wording to be verified against the KICD page.) Lesson question: How do we turn a real situation into a quadratic equation, and how do we know which solutions make sense?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 6 resolved the central puzzle: x(20 − x) = 96 gives x² − 20x + 96 = 0, (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, so x = 8 or 12, the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round. Lesson 7 shows that this is a general method by giving learners three new situations to form and solve (steps from L1 forming expressions from areas and L4 factorising). Learners meet two outcomes: a root that must be rejected (negative length) and a situation where both roots are valid (the ball at 15 m). This prepares Lesson 8, where they design a plot and explain why 105 m² is impossible. The DQB and the cumulative model gain a section on checking roots against the context.
slo.safetyNotes: Ball activity: do it outdoors on open ground at least 5 m from windows, people and roads, or use a paper ball or bean bag thrown gently upwards in the classroom with no one under it. Keep walkways clear of bags. Scissors for cutting grid paper: blunt-ended, used seated. Strings and loops kept off necks and not pulled tight. If no outdoor space exists, use the teacher demonstration plus the table of h-values only.

LESSONS.overview: Setting: Mama Wanjiru in Kericho now wants to use her mathematics beyond the vegetable plot. Her children Chebet and Kiprop tell her that the same steps she used for the 96 m² plot (write the area with x, set it equal to the target, rearrange to zero, factorise, check) can solve other questions. In this lesson learners work in groups of 4 through three situations: (a) a mandazi tray at a Kisumu market stall holding 60 mandazi in x rows and (x + 4) columns; (b) a path of uniform width w m around a 12 m by 8 m shamba in the Rift Valley, where shamba plus path covers 140 m²; (c) a football kicked at Kasarani whose height is h = 20t − 5t² metres after t seconds (g taken as 10 m/s²). Learners predict first, then form equations, solve by factorisation, and test every root against the situation. They find x = 6 (−10 rejected), w = 1 (−11 rejected), and t = 1 and t = 3 both valid for h = 15, and compare with the plot, where x = 8 and x = 12 were both valid but widths above 20 m were impossible. The phenomenon link: each equation arises from a fixed total (60 mandazi, 140 m², 15 m height) just as the fixed 40 m wire and 96 m² area did. The lesson ends with a DQB update and revision of the cumulative model to add the step 'check roots against the context'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the 40 m fence puzzle (x(20 − x) = 96 gives x = 8 and x = 12) and work individually for 3 minutes on a prediction card. Card: 'A Kisumu trader arranges 60 mandazi in a rectangle with x rows and 4 more columns than rows, so x rows and (x + 4) columns. Without calculating, predict: how many rows could there be? Could the answer be a negative number of rows? Why or why not?' Learners then predict about the ball: 'A ball kicked upwards reaches the height of 15 m. How many times do you think it passes the height 15 m, and when?' Learners record predictions with reasons in their books, then share with a partner (2 minutes).
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon picture of Mama Wanjiru's plot and the row of areas: '8 m gives 96 m², 12 m gives 96 m².' Say: 'Last lesson we solved x² − 20x + 96 = 0. Today we ask: how do we start from a story and get to an equation like that?' Read the mandazi situation aloud and draw a 3 by 5 tray on the board to show rows and columns. Say: 'Write your prediction quietly. You have three minutes. No talking yet.' WAIT TIME: after asking 'How many times does the ball pass 15 m?', wait 12 seconds in silence before taking answers. Then cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) for predictions on the number of rows and 3 learners for the ball. Record every prediction on the board WITHOUT saying which is right. Ask 2 learners: 'What made you think so?' Circulate and note the most common ideas, such as 'the answer is just 60 divided by 4' or 'negative is impossible'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Predict step): committing to a prediction in writing makes learners aware of what they currently believe, so later evidence can be compared with it. Recording all predictions publicly, without judging them, builds a class record of ideas to test and shows that mistakes are useful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who can name rows and columns as a product x(x + 4) in words or a sketch; (2) learners who treat negative as impossible for rows, which shows context sense; (3) learners who think the ball passes 15 m only once. Tick a checklist (names versus 'product idea', 'context sense', 'ball once or twice'). If more than a third of learners cannot link rows and columns to multiplication, revisit the 3 by 5 tray before moving on.

framework.learnerExperience: Stage A (about 7 min): Mandazi tray. Groups draw the tray with x rows and (x + 4) columns using squared paper (a 6 by 10 tray of squares is cut out to test). They write the equation x(x + 4) = 60, expand to x² + 4x = 60 and rearrange to x² + 4x − 60 = 0. Stage B (about 8 min): Path around the shamba. Groups draw a 12 m by 8 m rectangle (scale 1 cm = 1 m) and a path of uniform width w on all sides. They label the outer rectangle (12 + 2w) by (8 + 2w) and write (12 + 2w)(8 + 2w) = 140. They expand: 96 + 24w + 16w + 4w² = 140, which simplifies to 4w² + 40w − 44 = 0, then dividing by 4 gives w² + 10w − 11 = 0. Stage C (about 8 min): Thrown ball. Groups complete a table for h = 20t − 5t² at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (h = 0, 15, 20, 15, 0) and sketch the path of the ball. They notice h = 15 appears twice (t = 1 and t = 3), like the repeated area 96 m² in the fence table at x = 8 and x = 12. For each stage they record the variable definition, the equation, and the equation rearranged to zero. Note: the factorising is done in the Explain phase.
framework.teacherMoves: Give each group squared paper, a ruler, scissors (blunt) and a recording sheet with three columns: 'Define the variable', 'Write the equation', 'Rearrange to zero'. Say: 'Step one is always the same: say what your letter means, with units.' Model once at the board: 'Let x be the number of rows.' Circulate during Stage A and ask: 'If there are x rows, how many columns? How do you know?' During Stage B ask: 'Why is the path added twice to the length, not once?' (a path lies on both sides). Point to the drawing and wait 10 seconds for the answer. For Stage B support, hand out the pre-drawn outer rectangle. During Stage C say: 'Look at your table. Which height appears twice? What does that remind you of in our fence table?' Cold-call 3 groups to report the table and the repeated height. Deliberately do not factorise for groups yet. Check each group has written all three steps for each situation. Early finishers: write what x = 5 or x = 7 would give in the mandazi tray (x(x + 4) = 45 or 77), to confirm that only x = 6 gives 60.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling (Developing and using models): drawing the tray, path and ball path turns words into a picture and then an equation, so learners can see where each term comes from. Structured three-step recording (define, write, rearrange to zero) gives a repeatable routine, the same one used for x(20 − x) = 96. Comparing the repeated heights in the ball table with the repeated areas in the fence table builds the link that two answers can come from one equation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the variable is defined with units (e.g. 'w = width of path in metres'); (2) the outer dimensions of the path are written as 12 + 2w and 8 + 2w and not 12 + w; (3) the equation is rearranged to zero with correct signs (x² + 4x − 60 = 0; w² + 10w − 11 = 0); (4) the ball table shows h = 15 at t = 1 and t = 3. Use the recording sheets as a quick check. Common errors to note: writing (12 + w)(8 + w) for the path, forgetting to divide by 4, leaving the equation as x² + 4x = 60 and trying to factorise. Offer prompts rather than answers: 'Where is the path on each side?'

framework.learnerExperience: Groups factorise each equation and use the zero-product property from Lesson 6. Mandazi: x² + 4x − 60 = 0; two numbers with product −60 and sum +4 are +10 and −6, so (x + 10)(x − 6) = 0, x = −10 or x = 6. Path: w² + 10w − 11 = 0; numbers with product −11 and sum +10 are +11 and −1, so (w + 11)(w − 1) = 0, w = −11 or w = 1. Ball: 20t − 5t² = 15 gives 5t² − 20t + 15 = 0; dividing by 5 gives t² − 4t + 3 = 0, (t − 1)(t − 3) = 0, t = 1 or t = 3. Learners then complete a 'Keep or reject?' table: for each root they substitute into the original situation. The mandazi tray with x = −10 would mean −10 rows, so reject; x = 6 gives 6 rows of 10 mandazi (6 × 10 = 60). The path with w = −11 would be a negative width, so reject; w = 1 gives an outer size of 14 m by 10 m = 140 m². For the ball, t = 1 s (rising) and t = 3 s (falling) both give 15 m, since 20 − 5 = 15 and 60 − 45 = 15, so both are kept. Learners write one sentence per situation beginning 'I kept / rejected ... because ...'. They then link to the phenomenon: for Mama Wanjiru's plot both x = 8 and x = 12 were valid, but a width of 25 m would be rejected because the length 20 − 25 would be negative.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the sum-and-product method from earlier lessons. What two numbers multiply to −60 and add to 4?' Allow groups 3 minutes. Then cold-call 3 groups (one per situation) to write their factorised equations on the board while the rest check. Ask: 'Why do we get two answers each time? Which property tells us this?' WAIT 10 seconds, then take answers from 2 learners. Stress: 'Solving the equation is only half the job. Now we ask: does this answer make sense in the story?' Cold-call 4 learners: 'Can we have −10 rows of mandazi? Can a path have width −11 m?' For the ball ask: 'Is t = 3 an error because it is bigger than t = 1?' WAIT 12 seconds. Use a number line drawn on the board from 0 to 4 s with the ball path above it to show rising and falling. Challenge a group: 'Suppose someone says the ball reaches 25 m. Is that possible?' (set 20t − 5t² = 25, which gives t² − 4t + 5 = 0 with no suitable factors; use the table, where the maximum is 20 m at t = 2). Then connect: 'In the ball and fence situations the table shows a maximum, 20 m for the ball and 100 m² for the plot. That is why some targets are impossible, and we will use this in Lesson 8.' Do not teach the maximum method here, only note it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: for each root learners state a claim (keep or reject), give evidence (substituting back into the story: 6 × 10 = 60, 14 × 10 = 140, h = 15 at t = 1 and 3), and reasoning (a length or number of rows cannot be negative; both times are valid because the ball goes up and comes down). Comparing three contexts alongside the fence puzzle builds the idea that the mathematics gives candidates and the context decides which ones are answers.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) correct factorisations: (x + 10)(x − 6), (w + 11)(w − 1), (t − 1)(t − 3); (2) correct use of the zero-product property, with each bracket set to zero separately; (3) every rejection includes a reason in context words, not just 'it is negative'; (4) learners explain why the ball keeps both roots. Use a 3-question exit slip: (i) Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0 and state which roots make sense if x is a length in metres (x = 3; −5 rejected). (ii) Why does the ball have two valid times for 15 m? (iii) Why does Mama Wanjiru's plot have two valid widths? Sort slips into 'secure', 'partly' and 'needs support' piles for next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups revisit the class DQB. Each group writes on sticky notes (a) one question from today that is now answered (e.g. 'How do we turn a story into an equation?' answered with the three steps: define, write, rearrange to zero; 'Why do some roots get rejected?' answered by context checks) and (b) one new question for the next lesson (e.g. 'How can we design a plot for a target area?' or 'Why can't a fence of 40 m give 105 m²?' or 'Can any target between 0 and 100 m² be reached?'). They place answered notes in the 'We can explain' section and new notes under 'Still wondering'. The class reviews the original questions: 'Why do two plots have the same area?' (answered in L6 and revisited today), 'Why is there a maximum?' (partly answered, needs L8), and 'How can we find widths without trial and error?' (now answered for several situations).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes. Look at the board and our work. Write one question we can now answer and one we still wonder about.' WAIT 10 seconds before groups begin writing so everyone thinks. Cold-call 3 groups to read and place a note, and ask the class: 'Do you agree it is answered? What evidence do we have?' For each note, ask for the evidence from today's work. Highlight 'Why is there a maximum?' with a star and say: 'We have seen maximum values in the table for the plot (100 m²) and the ball (20 m). We will explain this fully in Lesson 8 with A = 100 − (x − 10)².' Do not explain it now. Praise precise questions and gently reword vague ones ('Why is there a limit to the area?').
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: tracking questions answered and unanswered makes growth in understanding visible and gives learners ownership of what comes next. Requiring evidence for 'answered' notes builds scientific habits of argument rather than accepting claims.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) answered notes cite evidence from today's equations (e.g. 'x = 6 because 6 × 10 = 60'); (2) new questions point to the maximum, target areas or impossible plots; (3) at least 3 groups raise a question related to the limit on area. Record which groups have only recall-level questions and prompt them with 'What would happen if the target were bigger?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the cumulative class model, which now has: v1 area models (L2), the three identities (L3), and two solutions (L6). New for Lesson 7: a 'Form and solve' flowchart: Read the story, define the variable with units, write the equation, rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0, factorise, use the zero-product property, check each root in the story, state the answer in a sentence. Learners add three worked examples around the plot model as evidence: mandazi x = 6 (−10 rejected), path w = 1 (−11 rejected), ball t = 1 and 3 (both kept). Each group also adds an arrow from the plot's valid range 0 < x < 20 to the idea 'context sets the allowed values'. Individually, learners write a short paragraph (3 to 4 sentences) titled 'How my model explains Mama Wanjiru's two equal-area plots and why I must check my answers', using the words quadratic equation, factorise, root and reject.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now do more than explain the 8 m and 12 m plots. It must show how to start from any story.' Display the blank flowchart and cold-call 5 learners to supply one step each in order, with the class giving thumbs up or down. Ask: 'Where on our model does the check against the story go?' WAIT 12 seconds. Then ask: 'If x = 25 were a root for the plot, what would we say?' (reject, the length 20 − 25 = −5 is negative). Walk round while learners write paragraphs and choose 2 to read aloud, asking the class to listen for the three required words. Collect the model sheets. Close with: 'Next lesson you will design your own plot for the school garden with a target area, and decide when no plot is possible.' Remind learners to bring their notebooks and grid paper.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative modelling: adding a procedure (the flowchart) and worked cases to the existing model shows how each lesson extends the previous one and connects to the phenomenon. Writing an explanation in own words consolidates understanding and lets the teacher see misconceptions, such as treating every root as an answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) the flowchart steps are in the right order, with 'rearrange to zero' before 'factorise' and 'check in context' after solving; (2) the paragraph correctly states that the two equal areas come from the roots x = 8 and x = 12 of the same equation (the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round) and that invalid roots are rejected; (3) the model includes all three situations with correct values (x = 6, w = 1, t = 1 and 3). Mark with a 3-level rubric: complete and accurate, mostly accurate, needs support. Plan a short reteach for learners who miss the context check.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson consider: (1) Which learners wrote (12 + w)(8 + w) for the path, and did the drawing with the path on both sides correct it? (2) Did learners see that rejecting a root is a mathematical decision based on the story, not a mistake in the algebra? Look at the justification sentences. (3) Did the ball example help learners accept that both roots can be valid? Which learners still thought one root had to be 'wrong'? (4) Was the time split between the three situations realistic? Consider giving the ball task as homework if time runs short. (5) Which groups struggled with factorising when the product was negative (−60, −11)? Plan extra sum-and-product practice. (6) What does the DQB show about readiness for Lesson 8, especially questions about the maximum area and impossible targets such as 105 m²? Note any misconceptions to address, for example that 'any area is possible if you choose x well'.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a worded situation (60 mandazi in x rows and (x + 4) columns; a path of width w around a 12 m by 8 m shamba with total area 140 m²; a ball with h = 20t − 5t²) can be written as an equation and rearranged to zero. We saw that the ball reaches 15 m twice (t = 1 and t = 3), like the 96 m² area appearing at x = 8 and x = 12 on the 40 m fence.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned the steps: define the variable with units, write the equation, rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0, factorise, use the zero-product property, then check each root in the situation. The mandazi equation x² + 4x − 60 = 0 gives (x + 10)(x − 6) = 0; the path equation w² + 10w − 11 = 0 gives (w + 11)(w − 1) = 0; the ball equation t² − 4t + 3 = 0 gives (t − 1)(t − 3) = 0.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that a quadratic equation can have two roots but the context decides which ones are answers: x = −10 rows and w = −11 m are rejected because lengths cannot be negative, so the answers are x = 6 and w = 1, while t = 1 s and t = 3 s are both kept because the ball goes up and comes down. This is why Mama Wanjiru's plot has two valid widths (x = 8 and x = 12, the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round) but widths above 20 m are impossible.

LESSONS.title: Applying and Synthesising: Design a School-Garden Plot and Explain the Maximum
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (2 x 40-minute lessons or one double lesson)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: quadratic equation, factorise, zero-product property, maximum area, A = 100 − (x − 10)², design, justify, reject invalid solution, Final Explanation, Driving Question Board, cumulative model

slo.purpose: Learners combine forming, factorising and solving to design and justify a school-garden plot for a target area and a fixed fence length, and explain why the area at a fixed fence length has a maximum of 100 m² at x = 10, completing the Final Explanation of Mama Wanjiru's plot in Kericho.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) form the area expression x(20 − x) = 20x − x² for a 40 m fence; (2) write a target-area equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 and factorise it, e.g. x² − 20x + 84 = 0 = (x − 6)(x − 14); (3) use the zero-product property to solve it and check both solutions against 0 < x < 20; (4) use A = 100 − (x − 10)² to explain why no area above 100 m² is possible, so a target of 105 m² is impossible; (5) explain why the widths x and 20 − x give the same rectangle turned round.
slo.skills: Mathematical modelling, forming equations, factorising, justifying and arguing from evidence, constructing explanations, revising a model, communicating reasoning orally and in writing.
slo.attitudes: Perseverance and integrity in checking solutions; responsibility and respect when critiquing peers' designs; appreciation of quadratic equations in real-life planning such as gardens, trays, paths and thrown balls. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration. Values: Responsibility, Integrity, Unity. PCIs: Education for Sustainable Development (school garden and food security); Life skills (decision making).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we form quadratic expressions and equations? Where do we apply quadratic equations in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. Lessons 1 to 7 gave us the area expression (L1), the squares identities (L2), the difference of two squares (L3), factorisation (L4, L5), solving by factorisation with two solutions (L6) and forming equations from situations and rejecting invalid answers (L7). Lesson 8 uses all of these in a new design task, finishes the Driving Question Board (DQB) and completes the cumulative model so learners can answer the driving question: how can we find the dimensions of a plot when its fence length and area are both fixed, and why do two different plots sometimes have the same area?
slo.safetyNotes: Use blunt-ended scissors and keep string loops, tiles and grid paper off the floor to avoid tripping. If measuring a real garden outdoors, stay within the marked area and carry tape measures carefully. Do not dig or fence any real ground without teacher and school permission.

LESSONS.overview: Mama Wanjiru's children, Chebet and Kipchop, found that with 40 m of wire an 8 m wide plot and a 12 m wide plot both enclose 96 m², while a 10 m wide plot gives 100 m² and widths above 20 m are impossible. In this final lesson learners act as designers for their own school garden. Each group is given a 40 m fence and a target area of 84 m². They form the equation x(20 − x) = 84, rearrange it to x² − 20x + 84 = 0, factorise it as (x − 6)(x − 14) = 0, solve it, and check that a 6 m by 14 m plot uses exactly 40 m of wire. They then test a second target of 105 m² and explain why it is impossible using A = 100 − (x − 10)², which is an identity check using Lessons 2 and 3 and not a new method. Learners complete the full area table, finalise the DQB and write the Final Explanation, comparing their Lesson 1 model with the final model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Mama Wanjiru's 40 m fence in Kericho. The teacher poses the school-garden challenge: 'The school wants a rectangular vegetable plot (sukuma wiki and spinach) using exactly 40 m of fencing wire. Could we get 84 m²? Could we get 105 m²?' Individually, learners write a prediction in their books for each target: possible or impossible? If possible, what widths might work? They give a reason in one sentence and note a confidence level from 1 to 5. Then they share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the challenge on the board and say: 'Remember Chebet and Kipchop's plots. Without calculating, predict whether each target can be reached with 40 m of wire. Write your reasoning.' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds of silent thinking before writing. Circulate and note predictions without confirming. Cold-call 3 pairs for the 84 m² target and 3 pairs for the 105 m² target, and ask each, 'What from our earlier evidence makes you say that?' Record the claims on the board in two columns (possible / impossible) without judging. Say: 'We will test every claim using our full model.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: learners commit to a claim before testing, so the final evidence either confirms or challenges their thinking and they see their own growth in understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) predictions that mention the 100 m² square at x = 10 or the table from Lesson 1; (2) use of the idea that length + width = 20; (3) misconceptions such as 'a longer fence always gives more area' or 'any target below 105 is possible'. Tally on a checklist how many learners predict 105 m² impossible and how many give a reason.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners design the plot. Step 1: Define the variable: width = x m, length = (20 − x) m because 2(length + width) = 40. Step 2: Form the equation x(20 − x) = 84. Step 3: Expand and rearrange to standard form: 20x − x² = 84, so x² − 20x + 84 = 0. Step 4: Factorise using the sum-and-product method: two numbers with sum −20 and product 84 are −6 and −14, so (x − 6)(x − 14) = 0. Step 5: Use the zero-product property: x = 6 or x = 14. Step 6: Check against 0 < x < 20: both are valid. A plot 6 m wide has length 14 m, and a plot 14 m wide has length 6 m, so it is the same 6 m by 14 m rectangle turned round. Step 7: Verify: 6 × 14 = 84 m² and 2(6 + 14) = 40 m. Groups build the plot with a 40 cm string loop (1 cm = 1 m) on grid paper. Step 8: Test the second target, 105 m²: x² − 20x + 105 = 0. Learners search for two numbers with sum −20 and product 105 and find none that work with whole numbers. They then complete the full area table from x = 2 to x = 18 (2, 36; 4, 64; 5, 75; 6, 84; 8, 96; 10, 100; 12, 96; 14, 84; 15, 75; 16, 64; 18, 36) and notice that the greatest value is 100.
framework.teacherMoves: Give each group a design card, a 40 cm string loop, grid paper, area tiles and the blank area table. Say: 'You are the garden planning committee. Show every step: variable, equation, standard form, factorise, solve, check.' Circulate and ask: 'How do you know the length is 20 − x?' and 'Why must we write the equation equal to zero before factorising?' For groups stuck on factor pairs, prompt: 'List the pairs of numbers that multiply to 84. Which pair adds to 20?' Give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each question before offering hints. For the 105 m² target, ask: 'What do you notice when you look for numbers that multiply to 105 and add to 20?' Do not tell them the answer yet. Ask each group to point to the largest value in their completed table and say what it tells them. Cold-call 4 groups to report the design result (width, length, check) and 2 groups to report what happened with 105 m².
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with mathematics and structured procedure: learners apply the full cycle (define, form, rearrange, factorise, solve, check) to a new situation, which shows that the same method resolves the original phenomenon and new designs. The area table gives numerical evidence that links to the algebra.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the group writes the length as (20 − x) before forming the equation; (2) the equation is rearranged correctly to x² − 20x + 84 = 0; (3) the factorisation (x − 6)(x − 14) is checked by expansion; (4) both solutions are checked against 0 < x < 20 and interpreted as one rectangle; (5) the learner reports that 105 m² has no valid width and links it to the table maximum of 100. Use a checklist with a tick for each step. Common errors to note: forgetting to rearrange to zero, sign errors such as (x + 6)(x + 14), or treating x = 6 and x = 14 as two different shapes.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners explain the maximum. The teacher writes A = 20x − x² on the board and asks whether it can equal 100 − (x − 10)². Learners expand (x − 10)² = x² − 20x + 100 using the identity (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² from Lesson 2, so 100 − (x − 10)² = 100 − x² + 20x − 100 + 100 = 20x − x²? They carefully work: 100 − (x² − 20x + 100) = 100 − x² + 20x − 100 = 20x − x². So A = 100 − (x − 10)². Pairs then answer: What is the smallest value (x − 10)² can take? (0, because a square cannot be negative.) So A is at most 100, reached when x = 10, a 10 m by 10 m square. Hence 105 m² is impossible and every width above 20 m gives a negative length. Learners also explain symmetry: A = 100 − (x − 10)² gives the same area for x = 10 + d and x = 10 − d, e.g. 12 and 8 both give 100 − 4 = 96, and 14 and 6 both give 100 − 16 = 84. Learners write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning paragraph answering: why do two widths give the same area, and why is there a maximum?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our table suggests a maximum of 100. Now let us prove it using what we know about squares.' Ask learners to expand (x − 10)² in pairs and cold-call 3 pairs for the result, with WAIT TIME of 10 seconds. Ask: 'Can (x − 10)² ever be negative? Why not?' Wait 15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'What is the biggest A can be?' Then challenge: 'Chebet says she can reach 105 m² if she is clever. What do you tell her?' Cold-call 2 learners. Show that x = 10 + 2 and x = 10 − 2 both give 96. Say: 'Be clear: the 8 m plot and the 12 m plot are the same rectangle turned round, not two shapes. A 4 m by 24 m plot also has 96 m² but needs 56 m of wire.' Do not teach completing the square or any formula; this is only an identity check using Lessons 2 and 3. Provide sentence starters: 'The area is greatest when... because...'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with an identity check: learners connect the numerical table (evidence) to the algebraic identity (reasoning) so the maximum and the symmetry are explained by structure and not only by pattern.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) correct expansion of (x − 10)² with the middle term −20x; (2) the statement that a square is never less than 0; (3) a conclusion that A ≤ 100 and equality only when x = 10; (4) a clear statement that x and 20 − x give the same rectangle; (5) rejection of 105 m² using the maximum. Score each CER paragraph with a 3-point rubric: claim stated, evidence from the table or equation, reasoning from the identity. Follow up with learners who say the 8 m and 12 m plots are different shapes.

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the DQB built across the unit. In groups, learners sort the question cards into: answered, partly answered and still open. For each answered question, they attach evidence from a lesson (for example the area table from L1, the squares identities from L2 and L3, the factorisation (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0 from L4 and L6, the rejected answers from L7 and the 84 m² and 105 m² designs from L8). They then write one new question about where else quadratic equations are used (for example the mandazi tray at a Kisumu market, a path around a shamba in the Rift Valley, a ball kicked at Kasarani) and add it to a 'Next questions' area.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take a card from the board. Do we have enough evidence to answer it? Show where.' Give each group 5 cards. After sorting, cold-call 5 groups to read one answered question with its evidence and 2 groups to read one open question. WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before each response. Ask: 'Which lesson gave us the evidence?' and 'What would convince a sceptic?' Move any question not fully answered to 'partly answered' and note what is missing. Praise precise evidence and ask learners to cite lesson ideas by name (for example 'zero-product property').
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board review: learners track and publicly connect questions to evidence, which shows the class how their understanding developed and identifies remaining gaps.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each answered card is linked to specific evidence and the correct lesson idea. Check that learners can say which questions remain open and why. A card sorted as 'answered' without evidence is a misconception flag. Record the number of cards correctly linked per group.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners complete the cumulative model. Each group takes their Lesson 1 model (area as width × length, x(20 − x) = 20x − x², first area table with 96 m² at 8 m and 12 m, 100 m² at 10 m) and compares it with the final model: area model of x(20 − x); identities (a + b)², (a − b)², a² − b²; factorisation of x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12); two solutions x = 8 and x = 12 as one rectangle turned round; checking against 0 < x < 20; and the maximum from A = 100 − (x − 10)², A ≤ 100. On a poster they draw both models side by side, listing what the Lesson 1 model could do and what the final model adds. Each learner then writes the Final Explanation individually: 'With 40 m of wire the length is 20 − x, so the area is x(20 − x). Setting it equal to a target area gives a quadratic equation that we factorise and solve. The two solutions x and 20 − x are the same rectangle turned round, so the area is symmetric about x = 10. The area is greatest, 100 m², at x = 10 because A = 100 − (x − 10)², and a square cannot be less than 0, so no area above 100 m² is possible.' Learners write it in their own words and include one worked design (6 m by 14 m for 84 m²).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Compare your first model with the model you have now. What can the new model do that the first could not?' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups to share one added feature. Ask: 'Which lesson gave you that feature?' Display the driving question and say: 'Use your model to answer both parts: how do we find the dimensions, and why do two plots have the same area?' Circulate during the Final Explanation writing and use the success criteria: variable defined, equation formed, factorised, both solutions checked, symmetry explained, maximum explained with the identity. Invite 3 volunteers to read their explanations. Close with: 'Where else in Kenya could you use this? Think of a mandazi tray in Kisumu or a ball kicked at Kasarani.' Collect the explanations for assessment.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with Final Explanation: comparing the first and final models makes the growth of understanding visible, and writing a coherent explanation consolidates the whole storyline into one answer to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-point rubric for the Final Explanation: (1) forms x(20 − x) from the 40 m fence; (2) forms, factorises and solves the target-area equation with a check; (3) explains the pair x and 20 − x as one rectangle turned round; (4) explains the maximum using A = 100 − (x − 10)². Model comparison: learners name at least 3 added features (the x² term, the identities, factorisation, two solutions, rejecting invalid ones, the maximum). Learners scoring below 3 receive a follow-up with the area table and tiles in the next lesson.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) How many groups completed all six steps of the design cycle (define, form, rearrange, factorise, solve, check) without prompting? (2) Did learners explain 8 m and 12 m as one rectangle turned round and not two shapes? (3) Could learners use (x − 10)² ≥ 0 to justify the maximum, or did they rely only on the table? (4) Which factorisation errors (sign errors, forgetting to rearrange to zero) remained? (5) How well did the DQB cards link to evidence from specific lessons? (6) Which learners need more support with forming equations from worded situations, and what resource (tiles, string loops, grid paper) helped them most? Note adjustments for the next unit, such as more practice with factor pairs or more time for the Final Explanation.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Core Mathematics Grade 10: Quadratic Expressions and Equations
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This Final Explanation is about Mama Wanjiru's vegetable plot in Kericho. She has exactly 40 m of fencing wire for a rectangular plot of sukuma wiki and spinach. Her children Chebet and Kiprop found that two different widths can give the same area. Use what you learned in Lessons 1 to 8 to answer each part. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Show your working, use units (m and m²), and check every answer against the situation. Refer to your Lesson 1 model and your final model where the questions ask you to.

sections.title: Part 1: Forming the area expression
sections.prompt:
Mama Wanjiru uses all 40 m of wire for the fence of a rectangular plot. Let the width be x m.
(a) Explain why the length is (20 − x) m.
(b) Write the area as an expression in x and expand it. Say why it is called a quadratic expression.
(c) Which widths x give a real plot? Explain why widths of 20 m or more do not.
(d) Use your expression to find the area when x = 8, x = 10 and x = 12.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The fence goes all round the plot, so 2(length + width) = 40. Therefore length + width = 20 m. If the width is x m, the length is (20 − x) m.
(b) Area = width × length = x(20 − x) = 20x − x² (m²). It is a quadratic expression because its highest power of x is 2. The x² term comes from multiplying x by a length that also contains x, which makes an x by x square region in the area model.
(c) Valid widths are 0 < x < 20. At x = 20 the length is 20 − 20 = 0, so there is no plot. Above 20 the length is negative, which is impossible.
(d) x = 8: 8 × 12 = 96 m². x = 10: 10 × 10 = 100 m². x = 12: 12 × 8 = 96 m².

sections.title: Part 2: Why two widths give one area
sections.prompt:
Chebet and Kiprop noticed that a plot 8 m wide and a plot 12 m wide have the same area.
(a) Write the equation you get when the area is 96 m² and rearrange it so that one side is zero.
(b) Factorise it and use the zero-product property to solve it. Show how you can check your answers.
(c) Are the 8 m and 12 m plots two different shapes? Explain using the length and width of each plot.
(d) Use the symmetry of the area table to predict one other pair of widths that give equal areas, and state that area.
sections.exemplar:
(a) x(20 − x) = 96 gives 20x − x² = 96, so x² − 20x + 96 = 0.
(b) We need two numbers with product 96 and sum −20. These are −8 and −12. So (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0. By the zero-product property, if p × q = 0 then p = 0 or q = 0, so x − 8 = 0 or x − 12 = 0, giving x = 8 or x = 12. Check: 8 × 12 = 96 and 12 × 8 = 96. Both are valid because 0 < x < 20. Expanding (x − 8)(x − 12) gives x² − 20x + 96, which also confirms the factorisation.
(c) No. When x = 8 the length is 12 m. When x = 12 the length is 8 m. Both are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle turned round. Width and length add up to 20 m, so x and 20 − x describe the same rectangle.
(d) For example x = 6 and x = 14 both give 84 m² (6 × 14 = 84). Another correct answer is x = 4 and x = 16, which both give 64 m². The areas are symmetric about x = 10.

sections.title: Part 3: Why there is a maximum area
sections.prompt:
With 40 m of wire, the plot with a width of 10 m gives the largest area.
(a) Which identities from Lessons 2 and 3 could help you show that the area x(20 − x) can be written as 100 − (x − 10)²? Write one of them in full.
(b) Show by expanding that 100 − (x − 10)² is equal to 20x − x².
(c) Use this form to explain why no plot can have an area greater than 100 m², and say what shape the plot is when the area is 100 m².
sections.exemplar:
(a) The identity (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² is used. The identity a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) is also part of the model.
(b) (x − 10)² = x² − 20x + 100. So 100 − (x − 10)² = 100 − x² + 20x − 100 = 20x − x². This equals x(20 − x).
(c) A = 100 − (x − 10)². A square (x − 10)² can never be less than 0, so we never subtract a negative amount from 100. Therefore A ≤ 100. The area equals 100 m² only when (x − 10)² = 0, so x = 10. Then the length is also 10 m, so the plot is a 10 m by 10 m square.

sections.title: Part 4: Designing a school-garden plot
sections.prompt:
Your group has 40 m of fencing wire for a school-garden plot.
(a) The target area is 84 m². Form the equation, solve it by factorisation, and state the dimensions of the plot. Check that it uses exactly 40 m of wire.
(b) A second group wants an area of 105 m². Decide whether this is possible and explain your reasoning.
sections.exemplar:
(a) x(20 − x) = 84, so x² − 20x + 84 = 0. We need two numbers with product 84 and sum −20: −6 and −14. So (x − 6)(x − 14) = 0, giving x = 6 or x = 14. Both are between 0 and 20. The plot is 6 m by 14 m. Check: area = 6 × 14 = 84 m². Wire = 2(6 + 14) = 40 m.
(b) It is not possible. The area is A = 100 − (x − 10)², so it cannot be more than 100 m², and 105 m² is bigger than 100 m². There is no width that gives this area with 40 m of wire.

sections.title: Part 5: Using the method in other situations and answering the driving question
sections.prompt:
A mandazi tray at a Kisumu market stall holds 60 mandazi in x rows and (x + 4) columns.
(a) Form and solve an equation for x. State which solution you keep and why.
(b) For a ball kicked at Kasarani, the height is h = 20t − 5t² metres after t seconds. The ball is at 15 m high at two times. Find both times and explain why both are valid.
(c) Now answer the driving question: How can quadratic expressions and equations be used to find the dimensions of a plot when its fence length and area are both fixed, and why do two different plots sometimes have the same area? Compare what you thought in Lesson 1 with what you know now.
sections.exemplar:
(a) x(x + 4) = 60, so x² + 4x − 60 = 0. Then (x + 10)(x − 6) = 0, so x = −10 or x = 6. We reject x = −10 because the number of rows cannot be negative. So x = 6: there are 6 rows of 10 mandazi (6 × 10 = 60).
(b) 20t − 5t² = 15 gives 5t² − 20t + 15 = 0, so t² − 4t + 3 = 0. Then (t − 1)(t − 3) = 0, so t = 1 s or t = 3 s. Check: 20 − 5 = 15 and 60 − 45 = 15. Both are valid because the ball is 15 m high once on the way up and once on the way down.
(c) With 40 m of wire the length is 20 − x, so the area is x(20 − x). To find the widths for a target area, we set the area equal to the target, rearrange to zero, factorise and use the zero-product property. For 96 m² this gives (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, so x = 8 or x = 12. Then we check the answers against 0 < x < 20. The two plots with equal area are the same rectangle (8 m by 12 m) turned round, because width + length = 20 m, so the area is symmetric about x = 10. The maximum area is 100 m² at x = 10 because A = 100 − (x − 10)² and a square cannot be less than 0. In Lesson 1 I could only find areas by trial and error and could not explain the pairs or the maximum. Now I can solve for the widths and explain both.
